title: Hippocratic Corpus
creator: hippocrates
location: Greek manuscripts; first printed edition Venice, 1526
note: Some sixty Greek medical writings that treat disease as a natural process to be observed, predicted and treated.
description: The Hippocratic Corpus is a collection of about sixty medical texts written in Ionic Greek by many authors, mostly between about 430 and 330 BC, and gathered under the name of Hippocrates, probably in Alexandria. Which, if any, Hippocrates wrote himself has been debated since antiquity. The treatises range from case histories in Epidemics and practical surgery on fractures and head wounds to theoretical works such as On the Nature of Man, which set out the theory of four humours, and On the Sacred Disease, which argues that epilepsy has natural causes like any other illness. Airs, Waters, Places links health to climate and environment, and the Aphorisms condense medical wisdom into short sayings, beginning with the famous observation that life is short and the art long. Preserved by Galen and by Arabic and Byzantine scholars, the corpus was the foundation of medical teaching in Europe until the seventeenth century.

image_caption: Part of an eleventh-century manuscript of Hippocratic works

title: Hippocratic Oath
creator: hippocrates
location: Part of the Hippocratic Corpus
note: An oath sworn by physicians to the healing gods, promising to help the sick, keep confidences and do no harm.
description: The Hippocratic Oath is one of the best-known texts of the Hippocratic Corpus, though its date and authorship are uncertain and it may reflect the views of only one group of physicians. The new doctor swears by Apollo, Asclepius and the healing goddesses to honour his teacher as a parent, to treat the sick by diet and regimen for their benefit and never to harm them, not to give a deadly drug or an abortive remedy, to leave cutting for stones to specialists, to avoid wrongdoing in patients' houses and to keep secret what he learns there. Byzantine scribes copied it, sometimes in the shape of a cross, and from the sixteenth century European medical schools adopted versions of it. Modernised oaths, such as the Declaration of Geneva of 1948, still carry its principles of beneficence and confidentiality.
image_file: Papyrus text; fragment of Hippocratic oath. Wellcome L0034090.jpg
image_caption: Papyrus fragment of the Hippocratic Oath

title: History of Animals
creator: aristotle
location: Greek manuscripts; Latin translation by Theodorus Gaza, 1476
note: A vast descriptive survey of animal anatomy, behaviour and reproduction, the founding work of zoology.
description: The History of Animals, in Greek Historia peri ta zoa, meaning inquiry into animals, collects observations on more than five hundred kinds of animal, many of them marine creatures studied around the lagoon of Pyrrha on Lesbos. Aristotle compares their parts, ways of life, habitats, feeding, breeding and character, drawing on dissection, the reports of fishermen and hunters, and earlier writers. Some observations were not confirmed for two thousand years, such as the placenta-like attachment of the young in the smooth dogfish and the arm used for mating by the octopus; others are mistaken. With its companion works On the Parts of Animals and On the Generation of Animals, it set out a programme of comparative biology. Through Arabic translations and Latin versions by Michael Scot and later Theodorus Gaza, it shaped natural history into the Renaissance, and Darwin praised Aristotle as one of the greatest observers.

image_caption: Twelfth-century Byzantine manuscript of the History of Animals, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence

title: Physics
creator: aristotle
location: Greek manuscripts; Latin translations from the 12th century
note: Aristotle's account of nature, change, causes, motion, place, time and the infinite.
description: Aristotle's Physics, from physis, nature, is a set of eight books of lectures on the principles of everything that changes. It defines nature as an inner source of motion and rest, distinguishes the four causes, material, formal, efficient and final, and analyses change, the infinite, place, void and time. Aristotle argues that a void is impossible, that a moving body needs a mover in contact with it, and, in the final books, that the eternal motion of the heavens requires an unmoved first mover. Together with On the Heavens, which described the four elements seeking their natural places at the centre of a spherical cosmos, it framed physics in the Islamic world and medieval Europe, where scholars wrote long commentaries on it and criticised its theory of projectiles. The new mechanics of Galileo and Newton was built largely in opposition to it.
image_caption: Opening page of the Physics in a printed Greek edition

title: Elements
creator: euclid
location: Alexandria; first printed edition Venice, 1482
note: Thirteen books building plane and solid geometry and number theory by proof from definitions and axioms.
description: Euclid's Elements, in Greek Stoicheia, gathers the mathematics of the Greek world into thirteen books. It starts from twenty-three definitions, five postulates and five common notions and proves 465 propositions from them in strict logical order: plane geometry, including Pythagoras' theorem, in the first books; proportion, probably following Eudoxus; number theory, with the proof that there are infinitely many primes and the Euclidean algorithm; incommensurable magnitudes; and solid geometry, ending with the five regular solids. The fifth or parallel postulate, which seemed less evident than the others, puzzled mathematicians for two thousand years until non-Euclidean geometries were found in the nineteenth century. Translated into Arabic in Baghdad and from Arabic into Latin by Adelard of Bath in the twelfth century, it was printed in Venice in 1482 and has appeared in more editions than any book except the Bible. It was the standard geometry textbook into the twentieth century.

image_caption: Papyrus fragment from Oxyrhynchus with a diagram from Book II of the Elements

title: On the Sphere and Cylinder
creator: archimedes
location: Syracuse; sent to Dositheus in Alexandria
note: Two books proving that a sphere has two-thirds the volume and surface of the cylinder that encloses it.
description: On the Sphere and Cylinder is a two-book treatise that Archimedes sent as a letter to the mathematician Dositheus in Alexandria. Using the method of exhaustion, squeezing a curved figure between inscribed and circumscribed shapes, he proved that the surface area of a sphere is four times that of its greatest circle, and that a sphere has two-thirds the volume and two-thirds the surface of the smallest cylinder that contains it. The second book solves problems such as cutting a sphere by a plane so that the two pieces have a given ratio. Archimedes regarded this as his finest result and, according to Cicero, asked for a sphere inscribed in a cylinder to be carved on his tomb; Cicero found the overgrown tomb in Syracuse by this sign. The treatise survived through Byzantine manuscripts, the commentary of Eutocius and Arabic and Latin translations.
image_file: Archimedes - On the Sphere and Cylinder.jpg
image_caption: Page from a copy of On the Sphere and Cylinder

title: On Floating Bodies
creator: archimedes
location: Syracuse
note: The founding work of hydrostatics, stating the principle that a body in a fluid is buoyed up by the weight of fluid it displaces.
description: In On Floating Bodies Archimedes treats fluids mathematically for the first time. Starting from a postulate about how pressure is transmitted in a fluid, the first book proves what is now called Archimedes' principle: a solid immersed in a fluid is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, so a body lighter than the fluid floats with just enough of itself submerged. The second book, a tour de force of geometry, finds the positions in which a floating paraboloid, a model of a ship's hull, is stable. The famous story of Archimedes discovering the principle in his bath while testing King Hiero's crown is told only by the Roman writer Vitruvius two centuries later and is probably a legend. The Greek text was long known only in a Latin translation by William of Moerbeke of 1269, until a Greek version was found in the Archimedes Palimpsest.
image_caption: A page of the Archimedes Palimpsest, source of the Greek text of On Floating Bodies

title: The Method of Mechanical Theorems (Archimedes Palimpsest)
creator: archimedes
type: Mathematical treatise in a palimpsest manuscript
location: Walters Art Museum, Baltimore (manuscript)
note: A lost treatise in which Archimedes explained how he discovered results by imagining figures balanced on a lever, recovered from a prayer book.
description: The Method, addressed to Eratosthenes, explains how Archimedes found his results before proving them rigorously: he imagined geometrical figures sliced into infinitely many thin sections and balanced against each other on a lever, a heuristic remarkably close to the integral calculus. It survives in only one copy, a tenth-century Byzantine manuscript whose parchment was scraped and reused in the thirteenth century for a prayer book. The Danish philologist Johan Ludvig Heiberg recognised the hidden text in Constantinople in 1906. The manuscript then disappeared, was damaged by mould and forged paintings, and reappeared at auction in 1998. Between 1999 and 2008, imaging with ultraviolet light, multispectral cameras and X-ray fluorescence at the Walters Art Museum recovered much more of The Method, the Greek text of On Floating Bodies and the Stomachion, a puzzle that may be an early study in combinatorics.
image_caption: A page of the Archimedes Palimpsest, with the prayer book written over the erased text

title: The Sand Reckoner
creator: archimedes
location: Syracuse; addressed to King Gelon II
note: A calculation of how many grains of sand would fill the universe, inventing a notation for enormous numbers.
description: In The Sand Reckoner, addressed to Gelon, son of King Hiero of Syracuse, Archimedes sets out to show that the number of grains of sand is not infinite, as some believed, but can be named. Greek numerals went only up to a myriad of myriads, a hundred million, so he built a system of orders and periods that can express numbers vastly larger, in effect working with powers of ten. He then estimated the size of the universe and found that it would hold fewer than about ten to the power of sixty-three grains. On the way he reports that Aristarchus of Samos had proposed that the Earth goes around the Sun, which is the main ancient testimony to that heliocentric hypothesis, and he describes his own measurement of the Sun's apparent diameter. It is one of the earliest works to discuss experimental error.
image_caption: Page from an early printed edition of The Sand Reckoner

title: Measurement of the Earth's circumference
creator: eratosthenes
location: Alexandria and Syene (Aswan), Egypt
note: Using the angle of the noon Sun at Alexandria and Syene, Eratosthenes calculated the size of the Earth.
description: Eratosthenes' treatise On the Measurement of the Earth is lost, but the Greek astronomer Cleomedes describes his method. At Syene, near the Tropic of Cancer, the Sun stood directly overhead at noon on the summer solstice and lit the bottom of a well, while at Alexandria, believed to lie due north, a vertical rod cast a shadow showing the Sun about one-fiftieth of a circle from the vertical. Since the Sun is so far away that its rays are effectively parallel, the arc between the two cities must be one-fiftieth of the Earth's circumference. Taking the distance as 5,000 stadia, he obtained 250,000 stadia, later adjusted to 252,000. How accurate this was depends on the length of the stadion he used, which is debated, but estimates fall within a few per cent to about fifteen per cent of the true value. The method is a classic of scientific reasoning and is still repeated by schoolchildren.

title: Discovery of the precession of the equinoxes
creator: hipparchus
location: Rhodes; reported in Ptolemy's Almagest
note: Comparing his star positions with older records, Hipparchus found that the equinoxes slowly shift against the stars.
description: Hipparchus measured the positions of stars relative to the equinoxes, the points where the Sun's path crosses the celestial equator, and compared them with observations made by Timocharis and Aristyllus in Alexandria about 150 years earlier. He found that the longitude of the star Spica had increased by about two degrees, and concluded that the equinoxes move slowly westward against the stars, by at least one degree a century; the true value is about one degree in 72 years. This also showed that the solar year measured by the seasons is slightly shorter than the year measured by the stars. His works On the Displacement of the Solstitial and Equinoctial Points and his star catalogue are lost, and we know them through Ptolemy. Precession is now explained, following Newton, as a slow wobble of the Earth's axis caused by the pull of the Sun and Moon on its equatorial bulge, with a period of about 26,000 years.

title: Antikythera mechanism
creator: antikythera-makers
location: National Archaeological Museum, Athens
note: A hand-cranked bronze device of interlocking gears that modelled the movements of the Sun, Moon and probably the planets.
description: The Antikythera mechanism was recovered in 1901 by sponge divers from a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, as a lump of corroded bronze and wood in 82 fragments. Decades of study, culminating in X-ray tomography and surface imaging from 2005, revealed at least thirty bronze gears in a box about the size of a shoebox. Turning a handle moved pointers on the front showing the positions of the Sun and Moon in the zodiac and the phase of the Moon, with a pin-and-slot gear reproducing the Moon's varying speed as described by Hipparchus; inscriptions suggest that it also showed the planets. Spiral dials on the back tracked the 19-year Metonic calendar, the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games and the 18-year Saros cycle for predicting eclipses. Its date is debated, with proposals from the late third to the early first century BC. Nothing of comparable complexity survives from the ancient world, and it has transformed views of ancient technology.
image_caption: Fragment A of the mechanism, National Archaeological Museum, Athens

title: Almagest
creator: ptolemy
location: Alexandria; Latin translation from Arabic by Gerard of Cremona, Toledo, 1175
note: The comprehensive Greek treatise of geocentric mathematical astronomy, standard for fourteen centuries.
description: Ptolemy called his thirteen-book treatise the Mathematical Syntaxis; Arabic translators knew it as al-majisti, the greatest, from which comes Almagest. Starting from the arguments that the heavens are spherical and the Earth stationary at the centre, it develops the trigonometry required, then constructs geometrical models for the Sun, the Moon, eclipses and each of the five planets, using eccentric circles, epicycles and the equant, a point from which a planet's motion appears uniform. It includes a catalogue of 1,022 stars in 48 constellations, largely based on Hipparchus. The models predicted positions well enough for practical astronomy and astrology for over a thousand years. Translated into Arabic in the ninth century and corrected by astronomers such as al-Battani, it reached Latin Europe through Gerard of Cremona's translation in Toledo. Copernicus, though he moved the Sun to the centre, followed its structure closely in De revolutionibus.
image_caption: Latin edition of the Almagest, 1515

title: Geography
creator: ptolemy
location: Alexandria; Latin translation Florence, c. 1406; first printed with maps, Bologna, 1477
note: A guide to drawing maps with latitude and longitude, listing coordinates for some 8,000 places.
description: Ptolemy's Geography, or Geographike hyphegesis, explains how to represent the spherical Earth on a flat map using two projections, and lists the latitude and longitude of about eight thousand places from the Atlantic to China, based on travellers' reports and earlier geographers such as Marinus of Tyre. Because it relied on itineraries rather than measurement, many positions are distorted; the Mediterranean is too long, and Asia stretches too far east, which helped Columbus believe Asia could be reached by sailing west. The text was rediscovered in Byzantium around 1300, and a Latin translation made in Florence around 1406 caused a sensation among Renaissance humanists. Printed editions with maps redrawn from its coordinates, from 1477 onwards, shaped European cartography until new discoveries made it obsolete, and its grid of coordinates became the basis of modern mapping.

image_caption: World map from a 15th-century manuscript of the Geography, British Library

title: On the Usefulness of the Parts of the Body
creator: galen
location: Rome; Latin translations from the 14th century
note: Galen's seventeen-book account of human anatomy as the perfect work of a wise creator, in which every part serves a purpose.
description: De usu partium, in Greek Peri chreias morion, is Galen's great work of functional anatomy, written in Rome. Book by book he describes the hand, arm, leg, organs of nutrition and breathing, heart, brain, nerves and eyes, explaining how each is perfectly designed for its purpose, in a spirit inspired by Plato and Aristotle that made it attractive to later Christian, Jewish and Muslim readers. His anatomy was based on careful dissection, but because human bodies were not available he relied on apes and other animals; he described, for example, the rete mirabile, a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain found in ungulates but not in humans. He believed that blood is made in the liver and consumed by the body, and that some passes through tiny pores in the wall between the ventricles of the heart. Vesalius exposed many of these errors in 1543, and Harvey overturned his physiology of the blood in 1628.

title: Edition of Ptolemy's Almagest (with Theon)
creator: hypatia
location: Alexandria
note: Hypatia is thought to have prepared the text of the third book of her father's commentary on the Almagest.
description: None of Hypatia's works survives under her own name, but the heading of the third book of Theon of Alexandria's commentary on Ptolemy's Almagest describes it as an edition revised by his daughter, the philosopher Hypatia. Scholars debate whether this means she edited the commentary or prepared the text of the Almagest itself, and some think the surviving text of Ptolemy may descend from her version. Ancient sources, especially the Byzantine Suda, also credit her with commentaries on the Arithmetica of Diophantus, a pioneering work on number problems, and on the Conics of Apollonius, and with an astronomical canon. Her pupil Synesius of Cyrene wrote to her about building an astrolabe and a hydrometer. Through such teaching and editing, the work of Greek mathematicians was preserved for Byzantine and later Arabic scholars.

title: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing (Al-jabr)
creator: al-khwarizmi
location: Baghdad; Latin translation by Robert of Chester, Segovia, 1145
note: The first systematic treatment of solving linear and quadratic equations, which gave algebra its name.
description: Al-Kitab al-mukhtasar fi hisab al-jabr wal-muqabala was written in Baghdad for the caliph al-Ma'mun as a practical handbook. Al-Khwarizmi reduced all linear and quadratic equations to six standard types and gave rules for solving each, justified by geometrical diagrams of completing the square. Al-jabr, restoring, refers to moving subtracted terms to the other side of an equation, and al-muqabala, balancing, to cancelling like terms. Everything is written in words, without symbols, and the book continues with applications to measurement, trade and the Islamic law of inheritance. It drew on Babylonian, Greek and Indian methods but organised them as an independent discipline. Latin translations by Robert of Chester in 1145 and Gerard of Cremona introduced the subject to Europe, where 'algebra' entered the vocabulary of mathematics.
image_file: Image-Al-Kitāb al-muḫtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-ğabr wa-l-muqābala.jpg
image_caption: Page from a manuscript of the Al-jabr

title: On Calculation with Hindu Numerals (Algoritmi de numero Indorum)
creator: al-khwarizmi
location: Baghdad; survives in a 12th-century Latin translation
note: The book that taught Europe decimal place-value arithmetic with Indian numerals and zero, and gave us the word algorithm.
description: Al-Khwarizmi's book on arithmetic with Indian numerals is lost in Arabic and survives only in a twelfth-century Latin version, probably made in Spain, which begins 'Dixit Algorizmi', thus spoke al-Khwarizmi. It explains the nine Indian digits and the small circle for zero, how place value works, and methods for addition, subtraction, halving, doubling, multiplication, division and square roots, as well as calculation with fractions. Indian mathematicians had developed decimal place value with zero by around the sixth century, and the system reached Baghdad by the eighth. Through this and related Latin treatises, the Hindu-Arabic numerals spread among European scholars, and the methods of calculating with them became known as algorism, the origin of the modern word algorithm. They took centuries to displace Roman numerals in everyday use.

title: Book of Optics (Kitab al-Manazir)
creator: ibn-al-haytham
location: Cairo; Latin translation De aspectibus c. 1200; printed Basel, 1572
note: Seven books showing that vision occurs when light from objects enters the eye, tested by systematic experiment.
description: In the Kitab al-Manazir Ibn al-Haytham combined the mathematical optics of Euclid and Ptolemy, the medical anatomy of the eye from Galen and the physical theories of the philosophers into a single new theory. He argued that every point of a visible object sends rays of light in all directions, and that vision occurs when the rays falling perpendicularly on the eye form an image of the object, rejecting the ancient idea that the eye emits rays. He investigated reflection and refraction in plane and curved mirrors and lenses, explained the camera obscura and visual illusions, and insisted that claims be tested by controlled experiments with tubes, screens and instruments. Translated into Latin around 1200 as De aspectibus or Perspectiva, under the name Alhazen, it was the foundation of medieval European optics in Roger Bacon, Witelo and John Pecham, and was printed by Friedrich Risner in 1572, when Kepler read it.
image_caption: Frontispiece of Risner's Latin edition, Opticae thesaurus, 1572

title: The Canon of Medicine
creator: avicenna
location: Persia; Latin translation by Gerard of Cremona, Toledo, 12th century; printed Milan, 1473
note: Five books organising the whole of Greek and Islamic medicine, the standard textbook in Europe until the 1600s.
description: Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb is a five-book encyclopedia completed around 1025. The first book covers the principles of medicine, from the humours and anatomy to the causes of disease and general therapy; the second lists some 800 simple drugs, with rules for testing their effects on the body; the third and fourth deal with diseases of each organ and those affecting the whole body, such as fevers; and the fifth with compound drugs. It synthesised Galen, Hippocrates, Aristotle and Persian and Indian sources into a clear, logical system, adding original observations, for example on the contagious nature of tuberculosis and the spread of disease through water and soil. Translated into Latin in Toledo in the twelfth century, it became the core of the medical curriculum at universities such as Montpellier and Leuven, with dozens of printed editions after 1473, and was still being taught in some places in the seventeenth century.
image_caption: Page from a manuscript of the Canon of Medicine

title: Liber Abaci
creator: fibonacci
location: Pisa
note: The book that introduced Hindu-Arabic numerals and their arithmetic to European merchants and mathematicians.
description: Liber Abaci, the Book of Calculation, opens by introducing the nine Indian figures and the sign 0, which in Arabic is called zephirum, and teaches how to read, write and calculate with them. Its fifteen chapters then apply the new arithmetic to practical commerce, including prices, currency exchange, barter, partnerships, alloys and interest, and to recreational problems and algebra drawn from Arabic sources. One problem asks how many pairs of rabbits will be produced in a year from one pair, if each pair produces a new pair every month from its second month; the answer generates the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and so on, later named after Fibonacci, though it was known earlier to Indian mathematicians. The book, surviving in a revised version of 1228, inspired the abacus schools of Italian merchant cities, where generations learned to calculate in the new numerals, and helped make Italy the centre of European mathematics.
image_caption: Page from a manuscript of Liber Abaci, Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale, Florence

title: Opus Majus
creator: roger-bacon
location: Paris; sent to Pope Clement IV
note: Bacon's plan for the reform of learning, arguing for languages, mathematics, optics and experimental science.
description: The Opus Majus, Greater Work, was written in great haste after Pope Clement IV asked Bacon in 1266 to send him his writings in secret. Its seven parts discuss the causes of error, the relation of philosophy to theology, the study of languages so that scripture and science could be read in the original, the usefulness of mathematics in every science, optics, which Bacon called perspectiva, 'experimental science', and moral philosophy. The section on optics, drawing on Ibn al-Haytham, describes vision, reflection, refraction, the rainbow and the use of lenses to magnify letters for those with weak sight. In the part on experimental science Bacon argues that arguments alone cannot give certainty without the verification of experience. The pope died in 1268 and there is no evidence that he read it. It was printed only in 1733, but it has been seen as a landmark in the medieval defence of mathematics and observation.
image_caption: Title page of a 1750 edition of the Opus Majus

title: Le Livre du ciel et du monde
creator: oresme
location: Paris; written for King Charles V
note: A French translation of Aristotle's On the Heavens with a commentary arguing that the Earth's daily rotation cannot be disproved.
description: Oresme translated Aristotle's On the Heavens into French for King Charles V and added a long commentary, finished in 1377. In its most famous passage he examines the question whether the Earth rotates daily while the heavens are at rest. He argues that all observations would look the same either way, since motion is relative, answering objections about falling stones and arrows shot into the air by pointing out that they share the Earth's motion. He adds that a rotating Earth would be simpler and more economical than turning the vast heavens. Yet he ends by saying that he believes, as is commonly held, that the heavens move and the Earth does not. The text also discusses the possibility of other worlds and compares the universe to a clock set going by God. Whether Copernicus knew Oresme's arguments is uncertain, but they show that medieval thinkers had already undermined some arguments against the Earth's motion.
image_caption: Miniature of the celestial spheres from a manuscript of Oresme

title: Anatomical drawings
creator: leonardo
type: Drawings in pen, ink and chalk
location: Royal Collection, Windsor Castle
note: Some of the most accurate anatomical drawings of the Renaissance, made from Leonardo's own dissections.
description: Leonardo's anatomical studies began in Milan in the late 1480s with drawings of the skull and became intensive around 1507–13, when he dissected human bodies at the hospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence and with the anatomist Marcantonio della Torre in Pavia. He drew the skeleton, muscles, heart, blood vessels, nerves and a fetus in the womb from several viewpoints, used cross-sections and exploded views, and made a wax cast of the ventricles of an ox brain. His studies of the heart describe the action of the valves and the eddies of blood in the aorta, in work that modern cardiologists have found remarkably perceptive, though he kept Galen's view of the blood's movement. He planned a treatise on anatomy that was never published. After his death the drawings passed to his pupil Francesco Melzi and later entered the English royal collection, where they remained largely unknown until the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

title: Codex Leicester
creator: leonardo
location: Private collection (Bill Gates)
note: Leonardo's notebook on water, the Earth and the Moon, explaining fossils and the glow of the Moon's dark side.
description: The Codex Leicester is a set of eighteen double sheets written in Leonardo's mirror script with sketches in the margins, named after the Earl of Leicester who bought it in 1719. Its main subject is water: how it moves in rivers and seas, forms eddies and waves, erodes mountains and might be controlled by engineering. Leonardo argues that fossil shells found high in the mountains were left by living creatures in ancient seas, not by Noah's flood, an insight that anticipated modern geology. He also explains the faint light on the dark part of the crescent Moon, the earthshine, as sunlight reflected from the Earth, a correct explanation later given by Kepler's teacher Maestlin. The codex was bought by the industrialist Armand Hammer in 1980 and by Bill Gates in 1994, the most expensive manuscript sold at that time, and it has been exhibited around the world.
image_caption: A page of the Codex Leicester

title: Commentariolus
creator: copernicus
location: Circulated in manuscript; first printed Vienna, 1878
note: A short manuscript sketch of Copernicus' Sun-centred astronomy, shared privately decades before De revolutionibus.
description: The Commentariolus, Little Commentary, was a short text that Copernicus circulated among friends without a title or his name some time before 1514, when a Kraków professor listed it in his library. It sets out seven assumptions: that there is no single centre for all the celestial spheres, that the centre of the Earth is not the centre of the universe, that the Sun is near the centre of the planetary spheres, that the distance to the stars is immeasurably greater than that to the Sun, that the daily motion of the heavens is due to the Earth's rotation, that the Sun's apparent annual motion results from the Earth's orbit, and that the apparent backward loops of the planets are caused by the Earth's own motion. It then describes the models with small epicycles that would replace Ptolemy's equant. Only three manuscript copies are known, rediscovered in the nineteenth century.
image_caption: Page of the Vienna manuscript of the Commentariolus

title: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
creator: copernicus
location: Nuremberg: Johannes Petreius
note: On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, which set out the heliocentric system in full.
description: De revolutionibus was printed in Nuremberg in 1543, after Copernicus' disciple Rheticus had persuaded him to publish and taken the manuscript to the printer. In six books, modelled on Ptolemy's Almagest, it argues that the Earth spins daily on its axis and orbits the Sun yearly with the other planets, then provides the mathematics and tables to compute their positions. The system explained naturally why Mercury and Venus are always near the Sun, why the planets seem to loop backwards, and gave their order and relative distances, but still used circles and epicycles and was no more accurate than Ptolemy's. A preface added without permission by the Lutheran theologian Andreas Osiander presented it as a calculating hypothesis rather than physical truth. The Catholic Church placed it on the Index pending correction in 1616. The historian Owen Gingerich's census of surviving copies showed that it was widely read and annotated by astronomers.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1543

title: De humani corporis fabrica
creator: vesalius
location: Basel: Johannes Oporinus
note: On the Fabric of the Human Body, a seven-book anatomy based on human dissection, with magnificent woodcuts.
description: The Fabrica, published in Basel in 1543, the same year as Copernicus' book, describes the human body in seven books on bones, muscles, blood vessels, nerves, abdominal organs, heart and lungs, and brain. It was based on Vesalius's own dissections in Padua, and he pointed out more than two hundred errors in Galen, showing that Galen had described animals rather than humans. Over two hundred woodcut illustrations, probably by artists in Titian's workshop including Jan Steven van Calcar, show skeletons and flayed 'muscle men' posed in Italian landscapes, and the title page depicts Vesalius dissecting before a crowd. The woodblocks were carefully cut and shipped across the Alps to the printer. The Fabrica, and the shorter Epitome for students, set a new standard for accuracy and illustration, and established the principle that anatomy must be learned from the body. The surviving blocks were destroyed in the bombing of Munich in 1944.
image_caption: Title page of the Fabrica, 1543, showing Vesalius dissecting before a crowd

title: De nova stella
creator: tycho-brahe
location: Copenhagen: Lorentz Benedicht
note: Tycho's report showing that the new star of 1572 lay far beyond the Moon, so the heavens could change.
description: On 11 November 1572 Tycho noticed a brilliant new star in Cassiopeia, as bright as Venus. Over the following months he measured its position with a large sextant and found that it showed no daily parallax, the shift that a nearby object would show as the Earth turned, and no motion against the stars. It must therefore lie beyond the Moon, among the fixed stars, contradicting the Aristotelian doctrine that the heavens are perfect and unchangeable. The star faded and disappeared by early 1574. Tycho's short book On the New Star, published in 1573, made his reputation and led to royal support for his observatory on Hven. The object is now known to have been a supernova, an exploding star, and is called Tycho's Supernova; its remnant has been studied with modern telescopes.
image_caption: Tycho's chart of Cassiopeia with the new star marked I, from De nova stella

title: Astronomiae instauratae mechanica
creator: tycho-brahe
location: Wandsbek, near Hamburg (printed by Tycho's own press)
note: Tycho's illustrated description of the instruments and observatories with which he made his precise observations.
description: Instruments for the Restored Astronomy was printed in 1598 after Tycho had left Denmark, as a lavish presentation volume to win the patronage of Emperor Rudolf II. It describes and illustrates with handsome hand-coloured woodcuts and engravings the instruments he had developed at Uraniborg and Stjerneborg, including great quadrants, sextants, armillary spheres and a large brass celestial globe, together with views of the buildings, and his autobiography. The most famous plate shows the mural quadrant, a large arc fixed to a wall, with Tycho pointing at the sky and his assistants at work in the observatory behind. The book explains how he improved accuracy, for example with new sights and transversal scales, and how errors could be checked by multiple instruments. It is a key document of the rise of precision measurement.
image_caption: The mural quadrant at Uraniborg, from Astronomiae instauratae mechanica

title: Mysterium Cosmographicum
creator: kepler
location: Tübingen: Georg Gruppenbach
note: Kepler's first book, explaining the spacing of the planets by nesting the five regular solids between their spheres.
description: The Cosmographic Mystery was Kepler's first book and the first openly Copernican treatise since De revolutionibus. Kepler believed he had discovered why there are exactly six planets and why they are spaced as they are: between the spheres of the planets, God had placed the five Platonic solids, cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron and octahedron, nested within one another. A famous fold-out plate shows this model, which Kepler even hoped to have made as a silver drinking bowl for the Duke of Württemberg. The scheme was wrong, but the book was significant because Kepler sought physical causes, suggesting that a force from the Sun drives the planets and weakens with distance. It brought him to the attention of Tycho Brahe and Galileo, and he republished it with notes in 1621, saying that almost all his later work had grown from it.
image_caption: Title page, 1596

title: Astronomia nova
creator: kepler
location: Heidelberg: Gotthard Vögelin (printed in Prague)
note: The New Astronomy, in which Kepler showed that Mars moves in an ellipse and set out his first two laws.
description: Astronomia nova grew out of Kepler's 'war with Mars', years of calculation using Tycho Brahe's observations of the planet whose orbit was hardest to fit. Kepler recounts his struggle step by step, including false starts: a model that fitted Tycho's positions to within eight minutes of arc was rejected because Tycho's data were better than that. He found that the planet's speed varies so that a line from the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times, and finally that the orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, the first two of Kepler's laws. The subtitle presents it as a celestial physics based on causes, with the Sun moving the planets by a magnetic-like force. The book broke with two thousand years of uniform circular motion and was the basis of the Rudolphine Tables of 1627, which proved far more accurate than earlier tables.
image_caption: Title page, 1609

title: Harmonices Mundi
creator: kepler
location: Linz: Johann Planck
note: The Harmony of the World, which contains Kepler's third law relating planetary periods and distances.
description: In The Harmony of the World Kepler pursued his lifelong belief that God created the cosmos according to geometrical and musical harmony. Its five books discuss regular polygons and solids, musical consonance, astrology and the motions of the planets, whose varying speeds he translated into musical intervals, giving each planet a melody and imagining the heavens singing in polyphony. Amid this, in the fifth book, he announced the discovery, made on 15 May 1618, that the squares of the planets' periods are proportional to the cubes of their mean distances from the Sun. This third law, along with the two of 1609, became the foundation of Newton's theory of gravitation. Kepler regarded the book as his greatest achievement, and its mixture of mysticism and mathematics shows how differently from modern scientists the founders of modern science could think.
image_caption: Title page, 1619

title: Galileo's telescopes
creator: galileo
location: Museo Galileo, Florence
note: The refracting telescopes, made by Galileo himself, with which he first studied the heavens systematically.
description: Hearing in 1609 of a Dutch spyglass that made distant objects appear near, Galileo worked out its principle and ground his own lenses in Padua, quickly improving the magnification from three to about twenty times. A convex objective lens and a concave eyepiece gave an upright image with a small field of view. He presented one to the Venetian Senate for its value at sea and in war, winning a salary increase, and then turned the instrument to the sky. Two of his telescopes survive in the Museo Galileo in Florence, one covered in paper and one in leather, together with the cracked objective lens of the instrument with which he discovered the moons of Jupiter. They are modest tubes of wood and paper about a metre long, but with them he discovered the mountains of the Moon, the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, sunspots and the countless stars of the Milky Way.
image_file: Galilei telescopes, Museo Galileo, Florence, Inv. 242, 2428, 224088.jpg
image_caption: Galileo's two surviving telescopes, Museo Galileo, Florence

title: Sidereus Nuncius
creator: galileo
location: Venice: Tommaso Baglioni
note: The Starry Messenger, announcing Galileo's first telescopic discoveries: mountains on the Moon, countless stars and four moons of Jupiter.
description: Sidereus Nuncius was a short Latin pamphlet printed in March 1610, a few weeks after Galileo's observations, in an edition of 550 copies that sold out at once. With engravings made from his own wash drawings, it showed that the Moon has mountains, valleys and craters like the Earth, whose heights he estimated from their shadows; that the telescope revealed vast numbers of stars invisible to the eye, and that the Milky Way is made of them; and, most sensationally, that Jupiter has four moons, which he named the Medicean Stars after the Medici rulers of Tuscany. Moons circling another planet showed that the Earth is not the only centre of motion and weakened a common objection to Copernicus. The book made Galileo famous across Europe, won him a post at the Medici court, and opened telescopic astronomy. Kepler quickly published an enthusiastic response.
image_caption: Title page, 1610, Houghton Library

title: Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems
creator: galileo
location: Florence: Giovanni Battista Landini
note: A dialogue in Italian comparing the Ptolemaic and Copernican systems, which led to Galileo's trial.
description: Written in Italian for a broad readership, the Dialogue presents four days of conversation in Venice between Salviati, who speaks for Galileo and Copernicus, Simplicio, a follower of Aristotle, and Sagredo, an intelligent layman. They examine Aristotle's arguments for an unchanging heaven and a stationary Earth, the evidence of the telescope and the problem of why we do not feel the Earth move, which Galileo answered with a principle of relativity of motion illustrated by a ship's cabin. In the final day Galileo presented his theory that the tides prove the Earth's motion, an argument that was wrong. Although the book had been licensed by the censors, it was taken as a clear defence of Copernicanism, and putting a favourite argument of Pope Urban VIII into the mouth of Simplicio was seen as an insult. Galileo was tried by the Inquisition in 1633, and the book was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books, where it remained until 1835.
image_caption: Title page, 1632

title: Two New Sciences
creator: galileo
location: Leiden: Elsevier
note: Galileo's final book, founding the sciences of the strength of materials and of motion, with the laws of falling bodies.
description: Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences was written while Galileo was under house arrest at Arcetri and, since he was forbidden to publish, smuggled out to the Protestant Netherlands and printed by Elsevier in Leiden. The same three speakers as in the Dialogue discuss the first science, the strength of materials, explaining why large animals and buildings need proportionally thicker supports, and the second, local motion. Galileo showed that freely falling bodies accelerate uniformly, so that distance increases with the square of time, which he tested by rolling balls down inclined planes, and that a projectile follows a parabola, combining uniform horizontal motion with accelerated fall. He also discussed pendulums and the paradoxes of infinite sets. The book founded the modern science of mechanics on which Newton built.
image_file: Galileo Galilei, Discorsi e Dimostrazioni Matematiche Intorno a Due Nuove Scienze, 1638 (1400x1400).png
image_caption: Title page, Leiden, 1638

title: Novum Organum
creator: francis-bacon
location: London: John Bill
note: The New Instrument, Bacon's plan for a method of inquiry based on careful observation and gradual induction.
description: Novum Organum was published as part of a vast unfinished project, the Great Instauration, for the renewal of all knowledge. Its title challenges Aristotle's logical works, known as the Organon, and its frontispiece shows a ship sailing beyond the Pillars of Hercules, the limits of the ancient world, with a motto from the Book of Daniel promising that many shall pass to and fro and knowledge shall increase. In a series of aphorisms Bacon criticises hasty generalisation and describes four kinds of 'idols', the illusions of human nature, of the individual, of language and of philosophical systems, that mislead the mind. He then proposes a method of collecting natural histories and arranging instances in tables of presence, absence and degree to arrive step by step at the causes of phenomena, illustrated with an inquiry into heat, which he concludes is a kind of motion. His method was rarely followed literally, but his ideals inspired the Royal Society.
image_caption: Frontispiece of the 1620 edition, Houghton Library

title: De motu cordis
creator: harvey
location: Frankfurt: William Fitzer
note: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood, demonstrating the circulation of the blood.
description: Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus is a short book of 72 pages printed in Frankfurt for the book fair. Harvey described his observations of the beating heart in many animals, including cold-blooded ones whose heartbeat is slow, and showed that the heart contracts actively to expel blood. He estimated how much blood the heart pumps with each beat and showed that in an hour it far exceeds the weight of the whole body, so blood cannot be continually made from food in the liver and consumed, as Galen taught, but must circulate. With simple experiments on ligatures on the arm, illustrated in the book, he showed that the valves in the veins allow blood to flow only towards the heart. Harvey could not see the connections between arteries and veins, which Marcello Malpighi observed with the microscope in 1661. Despite early ridicule, the circulation was widely accepted within a few decades and is the foundation of modern physiology.
image_file: Illustrations de Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis et sanguinis in animalibus... - (Non identifié) ; William Harvey, aut. du texte - btv1b2100015j (1 of 2).jpg
image_caption: Harvey's ligature experiments on the veins of the arm

title: La Géométrie
creator: descartes
location: Leiden: Jan Maire (appendix to the Discourse on Method)
note: Descartes's treatise joining algebra and geometry, so that curves could be studied through equations.
description: La Géométrie was the third of three essays published in French with the Discourse on Method in 1637, to show the power of Descartes's method. In three books he showed how geometrical problems can be translated into algebraic equations by assigning letters to lengths, and how equations can in turn be represented by curves, the basis of analytic or coordinate geometry; the familiar x and y axes were developed later by his followers. He solved the problem of Pappus, an ancient challenge, classified curves by the degree of their equations, and introduced the convention of using letters from the end of the alphabet for unknowns and from the beginning for known quantities, and superscripts for powers. Fermat developed similar ideas at the same time. Frans van Schooten's Latin edition with commentaries made it widely accessible, and it was the foundation from which Newton and Leibniz developed the calculus.
image_caption: Opening page of La Géométrie, 1637

title: Pascaline
creator: pascal
location: Surviving examples in the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris, and elsewhere
note: One of the first mechanical calculators, built by Pascal to help his father with tax accounts.
description: Pascal began designing a calculating machine in 1642, aged nineteen, to help his father, then supervising tax collection in Rouen. After some fifty prototypes he presented a finished machine in 1645 and obtained a royal privilege in 1649. It is a brass box with dials operated by a stylus; each dial turns a wheel, and an ingenious falling weight called a sautoir carries a one to the next wheel when a wheel passes nine, allowing reliable addition with carries across many digits. Subtraction was done by adding complements, and models for French currency had wheels for twenty sols and twelve deniers. About twenty machines were made, and nine survive. The Pascaline was expensive and delicate and sold poorly, but it was the first calculator to be produced in numbers and inspired Leibniz's stepped reckoner. The computer language Pascal is named in his honour.
image_caption: A Pascaline, Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris

title: Traité du triangle arithmétique
creator: pascal
location: Paris: Guillaume Desprez (posthumous)
note: Pascal's systematic treatise on the arithmetical triangle and its use in combinations and probability.
description: The arithmetical triangle, in which each number is the sum of the two above it, was known long before Pascal to mathematicians in India, Persia, China and Europe, where it appears for instance in the work of al-Karaji, Omar Khayyam and Yang Hui. Pascal's treatise, written in 1654 and printed after his death in 1665, gave the first systematic account of its properties and applications in Europe. He proved its properties using an early explicit statement of mathematical induction, and applied the triangle to combinations, the expansion of powers of binomials and the problem of points, how to divide the stakes fairly when a game of chance is interrupted, which he was discussing with Fermat at the same time. Because of this work the triangle is called Pascal's triangle in the West, though it is known as Yang Hui's triangle in China and Khayyam's in Iran.
image_file: FR-631136102 Em 0011 f 106 Triangulus Arithmeticus Definitiones.png
image_caption: Page from Pascal's treatise on the arithmetical triangle

title: Correspondence with Pascal on probability
creator: fermat
location: Toulouse and Paris; published in Fermat's Varia Opera, 1679
note: An exchange of letters that solved the problem of points and founded the mathematical theory of probability.
description: In the summer of 1654 Pascal and Fermat exchanged a series of letters about problems posed by the gambler Antoine Gombaud, the Chevalier de Méré. The central one, known since the fifteenth century, was the problem of points: how to divide the stakes fairly between two players when a game is broken off before either has won. Fermat solved it by listing all the possible ways the remaining rounds could turn out and counting those favourable to each player; Pascal used a recursive method based on expected values and his arithmetical triangle. Their letters agreed on the answers and established the idea that uncertain outcomes can be treated mathematically by counting equally possible cases. Huygens, hearing of their work in Paris, wrote the first published book on probability in 1657, and the subject was developed by Jacob Bernoulli, de Moivre and Laplace.

title: Fermat's Last Theorem (marginal note)
creator: fermat
location: Note in Fermat's copy of Diophantus' Arithmetica; published Toulouse, 1670
note: Fermat's claim that no three positive whole numbers satisfy x^n + y^n = z^n for n greater than two, proved only in 1994.
description: Around 1637, reading Claude Bachet's 1621 Latin edition of the Arithmetica of Diophantus, Fermat wrote in the margin beside a problem about dividing a square into two squares that it is impossible to divide a cube into two cubes, or any higher power into two like powers, adding that he had found a truly marvellous proof which the margin was too narrow to contain. His original copy is lost; the note is known because his son Samuel published an edition of Diophantus with his father's notes in 1670. Fermat did leave a proof for the case of fourth powers, but no general proof was ever found, and most mathematicians doubt he had one. Attempts to prove it over three centuries drove the development of algebraic number theory. The theorem was finally proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994, with help from Richard Taylor, using methods far beyond anything available to Fermat.
image_caption: Problem II.8 in the 1670 edition of Diophantus, with Fermat's note

title: New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air
creator: boyle
location: Oxford: H. Hall for Thomas Robinson
note: Boyle's experiments with the air pump on pressure, vacuum and life, from which came Boyle's law.
description: In New Experiments, Boyle described 43 experiments made with an air pump designed with Robert Hooke, a glass globe from which air could be largely removed. He showed that sound does not travel through a vacuum, that a feather and a coin fall at the same rate, that candles go out and small animals die without air, and that the mercury in a barometer placed inside falls as the air is pumped out, confirming that air pressure supports it. The second edition of 1662, answering critics, included measurements with a J-shaped tube showing that the volume of trapped air varies inversely with the pressure on it, the relation now known as Boyle's law; it had also been found by Richard Towneley and Henry Power, and was independently published by Edme Mariotte in 1676. Boyle's detailed, circumstantial style of reporting, written so that readers could virtually witness the experiments, became a model for scientific writing.
image_file: Boyle's first air pump. Wellcome M0010676.jpg
image_caption: Boyle's first air pump

title: The Sceptical Chymist
creator: boyle
location: London: J. Cadwell for J. Crooke
note: A dialogue attacking both Aristotle's four elements and the alchemists' three principles, arguing for experiment and atoms.
description: The Sceptical Chymist: or Chymico-Physical Doubts & Paradoxes is a dialogue among several speakers in which Carneades, Boyle's spokesman, questions the evidence for the two ruling theories of the composition of matter: the four Aristotelian elements, earth, water, air and fire, and the three principles of the followers of Paracelsus, salt, sulphur and mercury. Boyle argues that analysis by fire does not reveal the true components of bodies and that experiments do not support either theory. He favours a corpuscular philosophy in which matter is made of tiny particles whose size, shape and motion explain chemical properties, and gives a definition of elements as simple bodies not made of other bodies, while doubting that any such elements had yet been found. The book helped make chemistry a respectable branch of natural philosophy, though Boyle himself remained interested in alchemical transmutation all his life.
image_file: Sceptical chymist 1661 Boyle Title page AQ18 (3).jpg
image_caption: Title page, 1661

title: Horologium Oscillatorium
creator: huygens
location: Paris: F. Muguet
note: Huygens's mathematical theory of the pendulum clock, with results on curves and centrifugal force that influenced Newton.
description: Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656 and had it made by the clockmaker Salomon Coster in The Hague, reducing the error of the best clocks from about fifteen minutes to well under a minute a day. In Horologium Oscillatorium, published in Paris and dedicated to Louis XIV, he described improved clocks and provided their mathematical theory. He showed that a pendulum swinging in a circular arc is not exactly regular, but one swinging along a cycloid is, and he showed how to make it follow that curve with curved metal cheeks. On the way he developed the theory of evolutes of curves, found the formula for the period of a pendulum, analysed the compound pendulum and stated the laws of centrifugal force. The book was one of the most important works of mechanics before Newton's Principia, which owed much to it.
image_caption: Huygens's pendulum clock, from Horologium Oscillatorium

title: Treatise on Light
creator: huygens
location: Leiden: Pieter van der Aa
note: Huygens's wave theory of light, explaining reflection and refraction by the spreading of wavelets.
description: Huygens read his Traité de la lumière to the Paris Academy in 1679 but published it only in 1690. He proposed that light is a disturbance travelling at a finite speed through an elastic ether, and that each point on a wave front acts as the source of new spherical wavelets, whose common envelope forms the next wave front. This construction, Huygens's principle, gave elegant explanations of reflection and refraction, and he used it to explain the strange double refraction of Iceland spar, a crystal that splits light into two rays. His theory was eclipsed for a century by Newton's view that light consists of particles, but it was revived when Thomas Young and Augustin Fresnel showed in the early nineteenth century that light waves can interfere, and Huygens's principle remains part of optics today.
image_caption: Title page, 1690

title: Micrographia
creator: hooke
location: London: John Martyn and James Allestry, printers to the Royal Society
note: The first major book of microscope observations, with large engravings of a flea, a louse, a fly's eye and cork cells.
description: Micrographia, or Some Physiological Descriptions of Minute Bodies Made by Magnifying Glasses, was the first important publication of the Royal Society. Hooke described about sixty observations made with a compound microscope he had improved, of objects from the point of a needle and the edge of a razor to snowflakes, moulds, mineral crystals and insects, and some telescopic observations of the Moon and stars. In observing a slice of cork he saw tiny box-like compartments which he called cells, the origin of the biological term, though he saw only the empty walls of dead plant tissue. The large fold-out engravings, mostly from Hooke's own drawings, of a flea and a louse caused a sensation; Samuel Pepys sat up until two in the morning reading it and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read. Hooke also put forward ideas on light as a wave, combustion and the origin of fossils.
image_caption: Hooke's engraving of a flea

title: Letter on the 'little animals'
creator: leeuwenhoek
location: Delft; published in the Philosophical Transactions, London, 1677
note: Leeuwenhoek's report of single-celled organisms in water, the discovery of the microbial world.
description: In a long letter dated 9 October 1676 to Henry Oldenburg, secretary of the Royal Society, Leeuwenhoek described tiny living creatures that he had seen through his single-lens microscopes in rainwater, well water, sea water and water in which he had steeped pepper. He estimated their sizes, observed their movements and calculated that thousands would fit in a grain of sand. These 'animalcules' were protozoa and, in some cases, almost certainly bacteria. His claims were so astonishing that the Society asked Robert Hooke to confirm them, which he did in 1677 with witnesses' signatures. In later letters Leeuwenhoek described bacteria in the plaque of his own teeth, spermatozoa, red blood cells and capillaries. His instruments, of which about a dozen survive, were small brass plates holding a tiny lens, with which he achieved magnifications well above those of the compound microscopes of his day.

title: Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica
creator: newton
location: London: Joseph Streater for the Royal Society
note: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, setting out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
description: The Principia grew out of a visit by Edmond Halley to Cambridge in 1684 to ask Newton what orbit a planet would follow under a force decreasing with the square of distance; Newton replied that it would be an ellipse and spent the next two years writing the book, which Halley edited and paid to have printed. It opens with definitions and three laws of motion, including the law of inertia and the relation between force and change of motion. Book I develops the mathematics of motion under central forces, Book II treats motion in resisting media and refutes Descartes's vortices, and Book III, The System of the World, shows that a single universal gravitation, acting between all bodies in proportion to their masses and inversely as the square of their distance, explains Kepler's laws, the motions of the Moon and comets, the tides and the flattening of the Earth. Written largely in the language of geometry, it was hard reading, but it became the foundation of physics for two centuries. Revised editions appeared in 1713 and 1726.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1687

title: Opticks
creator: newton
location: London: Samuel Smith and Benjamin Walford, printers to the Royal Society
note: Newton's experiments showing that white light is a mixture of colours, with speculative 'Queries' on nature.
description: Opticks: or, a Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light was published in English the year after the death of Newton's rival Robert Hooke, though much of its content dated from experiments of the 1660s and 1670s. Using prisms, Newton showed that white sunlight is split into a spectrum of colours that cannot be further changed by a second prism, and that a second prism can recombine them into white, so that colour is a property of light, not something added by the prism. He explained the rainbow and the colours of thin films, including the rings now named after him, and described his reflecting telescope, built to avoid the colour fringes of lenses. In the Queries at the end, which grew with each edition, he speculated on the particle nature of light, the ether, chemical forces and the method of science. Written more accessibly than the Principia, the Opticks was a model of experimental science for the eighteenth century.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1704

title: Newton's reflecting telescope
creator: newton
location: Replica at the Royal Society, London
note: The first practical reflecting telescope, using a curved mirror instead of a lens to avoid colour fringes.
description: Newton's studies of colour convinced him that lens telescopes could never be free of chromatic aberration, the coloured fringes caused by different colours bending by different amounts. In 1668 he built a small telescope that used a concave mirror of speculum metal, an alloy of copper and tin that he cast and polished himself, to gather light, with a small flat mirror at an angle to send the image to an eyepiece in the side of the tube. Only about fifteen centimetres long, it magnified about forty times, as well as a refracting telescope several times its length. A second instrument was shown to the Royal Society in 1671, which led to Newton's election as a fellow and the publication of his theory of light. The design, now called the Newtonian telescope, remains popular with amateur astronomers, and all the largest modern telescopes are reflectors.
image_caption: Replica of Newton's reflecting telescope of 1668

title: Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis
creator: leibniz
location: Acta Eruditorum, Leipzig
note: The first published account of the differential calculus, introducing the notation dx and dy.
description: Leibniz's six-page paper, A New Method for Maxima and Minima, and for Tangents, which is not hindered by fractional or irrational quantities, appeared in the Leipzig journal Acta Eruditorum in October 1684. In compressed and sometimes obscure form, it gave rules for finding the differentials of sums, products, quotients, powers and roots, and showed how to use them to find tangents, maxima, minima and points of inflection, with applications to optics and geometry. Two years later he published the integral calculus, introducing the elongated S sign for summation. Leibniz had developed these methods in Paris in 1675–76, about a decade after Newton's unpublished work on fluxions. The bitter priority dispute that erupted around 1700, in which the Royal Society under Newton found Leibniz guilty of plagiarism, is now regarded as a case of independent discovery. Leibniz's notation, spread by the Bernoulli brothers and their pupils, became universal.
image_caption: First page of Nova methodus in the Acta Eruditorum, 1684

title: Explication de l'arithmétique binaire
creator: leibniz
location: Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences, Paris
note: Leibniz's account of binary arithmetic, using only 0 and 1, which he compared to the hexagrams of the Chinese Yijing.
description: Leibniz had worked on counting with only two digits since the 1670s, and in this paper for the Paris Academy he explained how all numbers can be written using only 0 and 1, and how addition, subtraction, multiplication and division can be done in this system, with remarkable regularities in the patterns. He had recently learned from the Jesuit missionary Joachim Bouvet in China about the 64 hexagrams of the Yijing, the Book of Changes, built from broken and unbroken lines, and argued that they matched the binary numbers from 0 to 63, which he took as evidence of ancient Chinese wisdom. Leibniz also saw religious meaning in binary, with all things created from one and nothing. The binary system had little practical use until the twentieth century, when Boolean logic and electronic switching made it the basis of all digital computers.

title: Marine chronometer H4
creator: harrison
location: National Maritime Museum, Royal Observatory, Greenwich
note: Harrison's large watch that kept time accurately enough at sea to determine longitude, winning him the Longitude Prize.
description: To find longitude at sea, a navigator needs to know the time at a reference place such as Greenwich while measuring local time by the Sun; each hour of difference corresponds to fifteen degrees. Pendulum clocks are useless on a rolling ship, and Harrison's first three sea clocks, H1 to H3, were large and complex machines with balances and springs. In H4, completed in 1759, he turned to a watch about thirteen centimetres across, with a fast-beating balance, diamond pallets and a mechanism to compensate for temperature. On a voyage to Jamaica in 1761–62 it lost only five seconds in 81 days, and a second trial to Barbados in 1764 confirmed its accuracy. The Board of Longitude demanded further proof and copies, and Harrison was fully rewarded only after appealing to George III and Parliament in 1773. Larcum Kendall's copy, K1, accompanied Captain Cook on his second voyage, and Harrison's ideas led to the chronometers that guided ships for two centuries. H1 to H4 are displayed at Greenwich.
image_caption: H4, National Maritime Museum, Greenwich

title: Solution of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg
creator: euler
location: Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae, Saint Petersburg (published 1741)
note: Euler's proof that no walk can cross each of Königsberg's seven bridges exactly once, founding graph theory.
description: The city of Königsberg in Prussia, now Kaliningrad, was built on both banks of the river Pregel and on two islands, joined by seven bridges, and its citizens wondered whether it was possible to walk through the city crossing each bridge exactly once. In a paper presented to the Saint Petersburg Academy in 1736, Euler showed that the answer depends only on how the land areas are connected, not on distances or shapes. Representing each area and its bridges, he showed that such a walk is possible only if no more than two areas have an odd number of bridges, and in Königsberg all four did. The reasoning, though Euler did not draw the diagram of points and lines now used, is regarded as the first theorem of graph theory and an early step towards topology, the study of properties unchanged by stretching. Two of the bridges were destroyed in the Second World War.
image_caption: The seven bridges of Königsberg

title: Introductio in analysin infinitorum
creator: euler
location: Lausanne: Marc-Michel Bousquet
note: Euler's introduction to analysis, which made the function the central concept and gave the formula linking e, i and trigonometry.
description: In the two volumes of the Introduction to the Analysis of the Infinite, Euler reorganised mathematics around the concept of the function, which he defined as an analytic expression of a variable quantity. The first volume treats exponential and logarithmic functions, defining them through infinite series and products, and establishes the number e, using that letter, as the base of natural logarithms. It presents Euler's formula connecting the exponential function with sine and cosine for imaginary numbers, from which follows the identity relating e, i, pi, 1 and 0. It also contains his solution of the Basel problem, the sum of the reciprocals of the squares, and the product formula linking the zeta function to prime numbers. The second volume covers analytic geometry of curves and surfaces. Written with great clarity, it was the model for mathematical textbooks for a century, and has been compared in importance to Euclid's Elements.
image_file: Introductio in analysin infinitorum. T. 1 - Leonhard Euler, 1748 (title page).jpg
image_caption: Title page of volume 1, 1748

title: Systema Naturae
creator: linnaeus
location: Leiden: Theodor Haak
note: Linnaeus's classification of the three kingdoms of nature, which grew from eleven pages to over two thousand.
description: The first edition of Systema Naturae, printed in Leiden when Linnaeus was a 28-year-old medical student, was just eleven large pages of tables classifying the three kingdoms of nature, animal, vegetable and mineral, into classes, orders, genera and species. Plants were sorted by their sexual system, the number and arrangement of their stamens and pistils, which made identification easy but caused offence to some readers for its frankness. Linnaeus revised and expanded it through twelve editions in his lifetime. The tenth edition of 1758–59, which consistently used two-word names for animals, is the official starting point of zoological nomenclature, as his Species Plantarum of 1753 is for plants. In it he placed humans with apes and monkeys in the order Primates under the name Homo sapiens. The hierarchy of ranks and the binomial system survive in modern biology, though the classification itself is now based on evolutionary relationships.
image_caption: Title page of the tenth edition, 1758

title: Species Plantarum
creator: linnaeus
location: Stockholm: Laurentius Salvius
note: Linnaeus's catalogue of all plant species then known, the official starting point of botanical names.
description: Species Plantarum, The Species of Plants, published in two volumes in 1753, describes about 5,900 species, everything Linnaeus knew of the world's flora, arranged by his sexual system. For each species he gave a short Latin descriptive phrase and, in the margin, a 'trivial name', a single word that combined with the genus name formed a convenient two-word label such as Bellis perennis for the daisy. Linnaeus meant these names as a practical shorthand, but they proved so useful that they replaced the long phrases. International rules of botanical nomenclature take 1 May 1753, the nominal publication date of this book, as the starting point for the names of most plants, so that many names still used today date from it. The specimens he used are preserved by the Linnean Society of London and are consulted to fix the meaning of names.
image_caption: Title page, 1753

title: Experiments and Observations on Electricity
creator: benjamin-franklin
location: London: E. Cave
note: Franklin's letters on electricity, proposing the single-fluid theory, positive and negative charge and the lightning rod.
description: Franklin's electrical letters, written to the London merchant and naturalist Peter Collinson from 1747, were collected and published in London in 1751, with later expanded editions, and translated into French in 1752. Franklin described experiments with Leyden jars, early capacitors, and explained electricity as a single subtle fluid present in all bodies, which could be in excess, which he called plus or positive, or in deficit, minus or negative, and which was never created or destroyed. He observed that pointed conductors draw off electricity silently and proposed that a pointed iron rod on a building, connected to the ground, could protect it from lightning, and that a rod on a high tower could test whether thunderclouds are electrified. In May 1752 Thomas-François Dalibard carried out the experiment at Marly near Paris, drawing sparks from a storm cloud, and Franklin's kite experiment in Philadelphia is said to have followed in June. The book made Franklin famous across Europe, and lightning rods spread rapidly.
image_caption: Title page, 1751

title: Traité élémentaire de chimie
creator: lavoisier
location: Paris: Cuchet
note: Lavoisier's textbook of the new chemistry, with a list of elements, the conservation of mass and plates of apparatus.
description: The Elementary Treatise of Chemistry, published in the year the French Revolution began, presented Lavoisier's new chemistry as a coherent system for students. Using the reformed nomenclature that he and his colleagues had introduced in 1787, it explained combustion, respiration and the calcination of metals as combination with oxygen, rejecting the phlogiston theory. It defined a chemical element practically, as any substance that has not yet been decomposed, and listed 33 of them, including oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and carbon, but also light and caloric, the supposed fluid of heat. It stated clearly that in every operation the quantity of matter is the same before and after, the principle of conservation of mass that underlies chemical equations. The second part describes the apparatus of the laboratory, illustrated by thirteen plates engraved from drawings by Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier. It was translated into English in 1790 and won over most chemists within a decade.
image_caption: From the Traité élémentaire de chimie, 1789

title: Traité de mécanique céleste
creator: laplace
location: Paris: J. B. M. Duprat and Courcier
note: Laplace's five-volume treatise extending Newtonian gravitation to the whole solar system.
description: Celestial Mechanics, published in five volumes between 1799 and 1825, gathered a century of work by Euler, Lagrange, Laplace himself and others into a systematic mathematical treatment of the solar system under Newton's law of gravitation, using the calculus rather than Newton's geometry. Laplace treated the shapes of the Earth and planets, the tides, the motion of the Moon, the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn's rings, and showed that the long-term inequalities in the motions of Jupiter and Saturn that had puzzled astronomers are periodic, so the solar system is stable. According to a well-known anecdote, Napoleon remarked that the work did not mention God and Laplace replied that he had had no need of that hypothesis; the story may have been embroidered. The book was translated into English with an extensive commentary by the American navigator Nathaniel Bowditch, and established the deterministic picture of a clockwork universe.
image_caption: From the first volume of Mécanique céleste

title: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae
creator: jenner
location: London: Sampson Low
note: Jenner's report that inoculation with cowpox protects against smallpox, the beginning of vaccination.
description: In May 1796 Jenner took matter from cowpox sores on the hand of a dairymaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inserted it into scratches on the arm of James Phipps, the eight-year-old son of his gardener. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with smallpox matter and no disease followed. The Royal Society declined to publish his short paper, so Jenner gathered more cases and in 1798 published this 75-page book at his own expense, with coloured plates of cowpox pustules on Sarah Nelmes's hand. He argued that cowpox, variolae vaccinae, gave lasting protection against smallpox without the dangers of variolation with smallpox itself. Despite opposition and caricatures showing vaccinated people sprouting cows, vaccination spread across Europe and the Americas within a few years, Napoleon had his army vaccinated, and Spain sent a vaccination expedition around its empire. Jenner's work led to the global eradication of smallpox, declared by the World Health Organization in 1980. The word vaccine was later generalised by Pasteur.
image_file: Jenner, An inquiry into the causes & effects Wellcome L0031742.jpg
image_caption: From Jenner's Inquiry, 1798

title: Essay on the Geography of Plants
creator: humboldt
location: Paris and Tübingen: F. Schoell and J. G. Cotta
note: Humboldt's study of how vegetation changes with altitude and climate, with his great cross-section of the Andes.
description: The Essai sur la géographie des plantes, written with Aimé Bonpland, was the first publication from Humboldt's American expedition. It is accompanied by a large engraved plate, the Tableau physique or Naturgemälde, showing a cross-section of the volcanoes Chimborazo and Cotopaxi in the Andes, with the names of plants written at the heights where they grow, and columns on either side giving, for each altitude, the temperature, air pressure, humidity, the blueness of the sky, the boiling point of water and other measurements. The plate showed at a glance how zones of vegetation are linked to climate and altitude, and how similar zones recur from the equator to the poles. It founded the science of plant geography, or biogeography, and expressed Humboldt's view of nature as an interconnected whole. In 1802 Humboldt and Bonpland had climbed to about 5,900 metres on Chimborazo, then believed the highest mountain on Earth, a record for decades.

title: Kosmos
creator: humboldt
location: Stuttgart and Tübingen: J. G. Cotta
note: Humboldt's attempt, in his old age, to describe the whole physical universe as a harmonious whole.
description: Kosmos: Entwurf einer physischen Weltbeschreibung, Sketch of a Physical Description of the Universe, grew out of popular lectures Humboldt gave in Berlin in 1827–28 and occupied him for the rest of his life; the fifth volume appeared after his death. The first volume surveyed the whole of nature, from nebulae and stars to the Earth's interior, magnetism, oceans, climate, plants and animals, while the second traced the history of humanity's understanding of nature and its expression in poetry, landscape painting and gardens. Later volumes treated astronomy and the Earth in detail. Humboldt wanted to show the unity of nature and the interconnection of all its phenomena, and to combine scientific precision with aesthetic feeling. Kosmos was a best-seller, translated into most European languages, and inspired scientists, writers and artists including Darwin, Thoreau and Frederic Edwin Church.
image_file: Atlas zu Alex. v. Humboldts kosmos 1851 (139502973).jpg
image_caption: Plate from the atlas to Humboldt's Kosmos, 1851

title: Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
creator: gauss
location: Leipzig: Gerhard Fleischer
note: Gauss's treatise on number theory, introducing modular arithmetic and making the subject a systematic discipline.
