description: The Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, Arithmetical Investigations, was written in Latin when Gauss was twenty-one and published in 1801 with funding from the Duke of Brunswick. It turned number theory, previously a collection of isolated results by Fermat, Euler, Lagrange and Legendre, into a coherent discipline. It introduced the notation of congruence, writing a ≡ b (mod m) when two numbers leave the same remainder on division by m, which made 'clock arithmetic' a powerful tool. It gave the first complete proof of the law of quadratic reciprocity, which Gauss called the golden theorem, developed the theory of quadratic forms, and in its final section explained which regular polygons can be constructed with ruler and compass, including the 17-sided polygon he had discovered at eighteen. Its compressed style made it hard reading, but it set the agenda of number theory throughout the nineteenth century.
image_caption: Title page, 1801

title: Theoria motus corporum coelestium
creator: gauss
location: Hamburg: Friedrich Perthes and I. H. Besser
note: Gauss's method for computing orbits from a few observations, with the method of least squares and the normal distribution of errors.
description: On 1 January 1801 Giuseppe Piazzi discovered a small new planet, Ceres, but lost it behind the glare of the Sun after observing it for only about forty days. Gauss, using new methods, calculated its orbit from these few observations and predicted where it would reappear, and astronomers found it there in December 1801, making him famous. The Theory of the Motion of Heavenly Bodies Moving about the Sun in Conic Sections, published in 1809, set out his methods for determining orbits. It included the method of least squares, for finding the best fit to observations affected by error, with a justification based on the assumption that errors follow what is now called the normal or Gaussian distribution. Legendre had published least squares in 1805, and Gauss's claim to have used it since 1795 led to a priority dispute. The method became the standard tool for analysing measurements in all the sciences.
image_file: Gauss, Carl Friedrich – Theoria motus corporum coelestium in sectionibus conicis solem ambientium, 1809 – BEIC 12217180.jpg
image_caption: Title page, 1809

title: A New System of Chemical Philosophy
creator: dalton
location: Manchester: R. Bickerstaff (London) and S. Russell (Manchester)
note: Dalton's statement of the chemical atomic theory, with the first table of relative atomic weights.
description: In the first part of A New System of Chemical Philosophy, published in 1808, Dalton set out the atomic theory he had been developing since about 1803. Each chemical element, he proposed, is made of identical atoms that cannot be created, destroyed or divided in chemical reactions, the atoms of different elements differ in weight, and compounds are formed when atoms combine in fixed simple ratios. This explained why elements combine in definite proportions, and why, when two elements form more than one compound, the amounts of one combining with a fixed amount of the other are in simple whole-number ratios, the law of multiple proportions. A plate showed his symbols for elements, circles with dots, lines or letters, and diagrams of compound atoms. Taking hydrogen as one, he gave a table of relative weights. Because he assumed the simplest formulas, such as HO for water, many of his weights were wrong, and it took half a century to agree on correct values, but his theory became the foundation of chemistry.

title: Discovery of electromagnetic induction
creator: faraday
location: Royal Institution, London; published in the Philosophical Transactions, 1832
note: Faraday showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric current, the principle of the generator and transformer.
description: After Hans Christian Ørsted showed in 1820 that an electric current deflects a compass needle, many tried to find the reverse effect, electricity from magnetism. On 29 August 1831 Faraday wound two coils of insulated wire on opposite sides of an iron ring and found that when he switched on or off the current in one coil, a brief current flowed in the other, but none while the current was steady. Over the following weeks he showed that moving a magnet into or out of a coil also produced a current, and that a copper disc rotating between the poles of a magnet gave a continuous current, the first dynamo. He reported the results to the Royal Society in November as the first series of his Experimental Researches in Electricity. Induction is the principle of the electric generator and the transformer, on which electric power systems depend. Joseph Henry in America discovered it independently at about the same time. The induction ring survives at the Royal Institution.
image_caption: Faraday's induction ring of 1831

title: The Chemical History of a Candle
creator: faraday
location: Royal Institution, London; published London: Griffin, Bohn
note: Faraday's Christmas lectures explaining the science of a burning candle, a classic of popular science.
description: Faraday gave the Royal Institution's Christmas lectures for young people nineteen times, and his series on The Chemical History of a Candle, first given in 1848 and repeated in 1860–61, became the most famous. In six lectures he used the burning candle to explain capillary action, the shape of the flame, the products of combustion, the composition of water and air, the properties of hydrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide, and finally respiration, comparing the slow burning of carbon in our bodies to the candle. Each lecture was full of demonstrations. The lectures were taken down in shorthand by William Crookes and published in 1861, and have been in print ever since in many languages. Faraday ended by wishing that his listeners might, like the candle, shine as lights to those about them. The Christmas lectures continue today, broadcast on television.

title: Principles of Geology
creator: lyell
location: London: John Murray
note: Lyell's argument that the Earth's surface was shaped over vast time by causes still operating today.
description: Principles of Geology, being an Attempt to Explain the Former Changes of the Earth's Surface, by Reference to Causes now in Operation, was published in three volumes and revised through twelve editions in Lyell's lifetime. Against geologists who explained mountains, valleys and fossil extinctions by past catastrophes far more violent than any seen today, Lyell argued that ordinary processes, erosion, sedimentation, earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, acting over immense periods of time, were sufficient to explain everything. The frontispiece shows the columns of the so-called Temple of Serapis at Pozzuoli near Naples, bored by marine molluscs, as evidence that the land had slowly sunk beneath the sea and risen again. The second volume discussed the distribution and extinction of species, though Lyell then rejected transmutation. Darwin took the first volume on the Beagle and saw the land through Lyell's eyes; the long timescale Lyell established was essential to the theory of evolution.
image_caption: Frontispiece: the columns of the 'Temple of Serapis' at Pozzuoli

title: Journal of Researches (The Voyage of the Beagle)
creator: darwin
location: London: Henry Colburn
note: Darwin's account of his five-year voyage round the world on HMS Beagle, including the Galápagos Islands.
description: Darwin's journal of the voyage of HMS Beagle, 1831–36, was first published in 1839 as the third volume of the official narrative of the expedition, edited by Captain Robert FitzRoy, and was so popular that it was reissued separately the same year; a revised edition of 1845 added more about evolution in all but name. It describes the geology, plants, animals and peoples of the places he visited: the fossils of giant extinct mammals in Argentina, the rise of the Chilean coast after an earthquake, the Andes, the coral reefs of the Indian Ocean, which he explained by the slow sinking of islands, and the Galápagos, where he noted that the islands had distinct forms of tortoises, mockingbirds and finches. It made his reputation as a naturalist and writer and is still read as one of the great travel books. Its observations of species varying from place to place were among the seeds of his theory of natural selection.
image_caption: From an early edition of Darwin's Journal

title: 'I think' tree sketch (Notebook B)
creator: darwin
location: Cambridge University Library
note: A small branching diagram in Darwin's private notebook, his first sketch of an evolutionary tree of life.
description: In July 1837, back in London, Darwin began a series of private notebooks on the 'transmutation of species'. On page 36 of the first of them, Notebook B, he wrote the words 'I think' and below them drew a small branching tree, with a single trunk dividing into branches, some ending in lines and some marked with letters, to show how species might be related by common descent, with extinct forms explaining the gaps between living groups. It is his earliest known diagram of evolution as a branching process rather than a ladder, and it anticipates the only illustration in On the Origin of Species, a more abstract tree. The notebook was among two that went missing from Cambridge University Library around 2000 and were returned anonymously, in good condition, in 2022.
image_caption: Darwin's 'I think' sketch, Notebook B, 1837

title: On the Origin of Species
creator: darwin
location: London: John Murray
note: Darwin's theory that species evolve by natural selection, descending with modification from common ancestors.
description: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life was published on 24 November 1859, and its first printing of 1,250 copies was taken up by booksellers on the first day. Darwin, prompted by Alfred Russel Wallace's independent discovery, presented what he called one long argument. Starting from the variation produced by breeders of pigeons and other domestic animals, he argued that in nature more individuals are born than can survive, so those with variations better suited to their conditions tend to leave more offspring, and over long periods this natural selection produces new species. He showed how the theory explained the geological record, the geographical distribution of species, classification, embryology and rudimentary organs, and frankly discussed difficulties such as the evolution of the eye. He said almost nothing about humans. The book provoked fierce debate, but within two decades most scientists accepted evolution. It went through six editions, in which Darwin answered critics.
image_caption: Title page of the first edition, 1859

title: The Descent of Man
creator: darwin
location: London: John Murray
note: Darwin's application of evolution to humans, and his theory of sexual selection.
description: The Descent of Man, and Selection in Relation to Sex applied the theory of evolution to the human species, which Darwin had avoided discussing in the Origin. He argued, from anatomy, embryology and rudimentary organs, that humans are descended from an ancestor shared with the apes, probably in Africa, and that human mental and moral faculties, including conscience and sympathy, differ from those of animals in degree rather than kind. Most of the book develops the theory of sexual selection: traits such as the peacock's tail, the antlers of deer and the songs of birds evolved because they helped individuals win mates, either by attracting the opposite sex or by defeating rivals. Darwin used it to explain differences between human populations and between the sexes, in passages that reflect the racial and gender assumptions of Victorian England and have been much criticised. Sexual selection, neglected for a century, is now a major field of evolutionary biology.
image_caption: Title page, 1871

title: Experiments on Plant Hybridization
creator: mendel
location: Verhandlungen des naturforschenden Vereines in Brünn
note: Mendel's paper on crossing peas, which revealed the statistical laws of inheritance.
description: Versuche über Pflanzenhybriden reported eight years of experiments in the abbey garden at Brno with some 28,000 pea plants. Mendel chose seven characters that appeared in two clear forms, such as round or wrinkled seeds and tall or short stems, crossed pure-breeding plants, and counted the offspring over several generations. In the first generation all plants showed one form, the dominant; in the next the recessive form reappeared in about a quarter of the plants, a ratio of three to one. He explained this by hereditary elements that come in pairs and separate when germ cells form, and showed that different characters are inherited independently of each other. He read the paper to the Natural History Society of Brno in 1865 and it was published in 1866, but its significance was not recognised. In 1900 Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak independently rediscovered it, and it became the foundation of genetics. Statisticians including R. A. Fisher later suggested that his data fit the expected ratios suspiciously well, a question still discussed.
image_caption: First page of Mendel's paper

title: Swan-neck flask experiments
creator: pasteur
location: École normale supérieure, Paris; Institut Pasteur, Paris (original flasks)
note: Pasteur's experiments showing that broth stays sterile if dust is kept out, refuting spontaneous generation.
description: The question of whether living things can arise spontaneously from non-living matter was revived in 1859 by the naturalist Félix Pouchet, and the French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for experiments that would settle it. Pasteur boiled nutrient broth in flasks whose necks he had drawn out into long S-shaped curves, open to the air. Dust and microbes settled in the bend and did not reach the liquid, which remained clear indefinitely; when the neck was broken off or the flask tilted so that broth touched the trapped dust, it soon teemed with life. He also exposed flasks to air at different altitudes, including on a glacier near Mont Blanc, and found fewer contaminations in pure mountain air. He won the prize in 1862 and announced in a lecture at the Sorbonne in 1864 that spontaneous generation would never recover. The experiments supported his germ theory of fermentation and disease. Some of the original flasks, still sterile, are kept at the Institut Pasteur.
image_file: Swan-necked flask used by Pasteur. Wellcome M0012521.jpg
image_caption: Swan-necked flask used by Pasteur

title: Rabies vaccine
creator: pasteur
location: Laboratory of the École normale supérieure, Paris
note: The first vaccine against rabies, given in 1885 to a boy bitten by a rabid dog.
description: Rabies was then always fatal once symptoms appeared. Pasteur and his collaborators, especially Émile Roux, could not see the infectious agent, which is a virus, but they passed it through rabbits and weakened it by drying the infected spinal cords in sealed flasks for different numbers of days. Because rabies takes weeks to develop, they reasoned that a series of injections of increasingly virulent material might produce immunity after a bite. On 6 July 1885 a nine-year-old Alsatian boy, Joseph Meister, was brought to Paris two days after being badly bitten by a rabid dog, and Pasteur, who was not a physician, had doctors give him thirteen injections over ten days. The boy survived, as did a young shepherd, Jean-Baptiste Jupille, treated in October. News spread, and patients came from around the world. The success led to the founding of the Institut Pasteur in 1888. Historians studying his notebooks have shown that the vaccine had been less thoroughly tested in animals than he publicly implied.

title: A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field
creator: maxwell
location: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London
note: Maxwell's paper setting out the equations of the electromagnetic field and identifying light as an electromagnetic wave.
description: Maxwell read this paper to the Royal Society in December 1864 and published it in 1865. Earlier he had modelled Faraday's lines of force with an imaginary mechanism of spinning vortices, and had found that it predicted waves travelling at the speed of light. In this paper he dropped the mechanical model and described the electromagnetic field directly by twenty equations relating electric and magnetic forces, currents and charges, including the displacement current he had introduced. From them he derived waves of electric and magnetic disturbance travelling at a speed that matched the measured speed of light, and concluded that light itself is an electromagnetic disturbance. Oliver Heaviside later condensed the equations into the four now known as Maxwell's equations. Heinrich Hertz produced and detected electromagnetic waves in 1887–88, leading to radio, and the theory raised the questions about the speed of light that Einstein answered with relativity.

title: A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism
creator: maxwell
location: Oxford: Clarendon Press
note: Maxwell's comprehensive treatise on electromagnetism, from which a generation of physicists learned field theory.
description: In the two volumes of the Treatise, Maxwell gathered the whole of electricity and magnetism, experimental and theoretical, into a single system based on the field. He covered electrostatics, electric currents, magnetism and electromagnetism, treated mathematical methods such as potential theory and spherical harmonics, described measuring instruments, and set out his electromagnetic theory of light. He predicted that light would exert a pressure on surfaces it falls on, which was later confirmed. The book was difficult and in places obscure, and much of the work of the following generation, by Heaviside, Hertz, George FitzGerald, Oliver Lodge and others, the so-called Maxwellians, consisted of clarifying and simplifying it. Einstein later called the change from action at a distance to fields the most profound since Newton.

title: First colour photograph (tartan ribbon)
creator: maxwell
location: Royal Institution, London; plates at the James Clerk Maxwell Foundation, Edinburgh
note: A demonstration of the three-colour method of colour photography that Maxwell proposed in 1855.
description: Maxwell's studies of colour vision showed that any colour the eye perceives can be matched by mixing three primary lights, red, green and blue. In 1855 he suggested that a colour photograph could be made by taking three black-and-white photographs through red, green and blue filters, and projecting them superimposed through the same filters. For a lecture at the Royal Institution in May 1861, the photographer Thomas Sutton photographed a tartan ribbon in this way, and the projected image reproduced its colours. The result was better than it should have been, because the photographic emulsions of the time were barely sensitive to red; a century later it was found that the red filter had passed ultraviolet light reflected by the red dyes. The three-colour principle underlies colour photography, television and digital screens.
image_caption: The tartan ribbon, projected by Maxwell in 1861

title: Periodic table of the elements
creator: mendeleev
location: Saint Petersburg; published in the Zhurnal Russkogo Khimicheskogo Obshchestva and Zeitschrift für Chemie
note: Mendeleev's arrangement of the elements by atomic weight and properties, with gaps for undiscovered elements.
description: In February 1869, while writing his textbook, Mendeleev drew up a table of the 63 known elements in order of atomic weight, arranged so that elements with similar properties, such as the alkali metals or the halogens, fell into the same groups. He printed it as a single sheet titled An Attempt at a System of Elements, and presented a paper on it to the Russian Chemical Society in March. Where the order of weights clashed with chemical properties, he trusted the properties and suggested the weights were wrong, and he left gaps for missing elements. In 1871 he predicted in detail the properties of three of them, which he called eka-aluminium, eka-boron and eka-silicon. Gallium was discovered in 1875, scandium in 1879 and germanium in 1886, with properties closely matching his predictions. Later work showed that the order is set by atomic number, the charge of the nucleus, and the table's structure was explained by quantum mechanics. It is the central icon of chemistry.
image_caption: A modern form of the periodic table

title: On the Antiseptic Principle in the Practice of Surgery
creator: lister
location: The Lancet, London
note: Lister's reports on preventing wound infection with carbolic acid, founding antiseptic surgery.
description: In the mid nineteenth century almost half of patients who had a limb amputated in some hospitals died of infection, and 'hospital gangrene' was widely blamed on bad air. At Glasgow Royal Infirmary, Lister read Pasteur's work showing that fermentation and putrefaction are caused by microbes, and reasoned that germs entering wounds caused sepsis. In August 1865 he treated a boy's compound fracture of the leg, in which the bone had broken the skin, with lint soaked in carbolic acid, a chemical used to treat sewage, and the wound healed without infection. In a series of articles in The Lancet in 1867 he reported his results with compound fractures and abscesses, and in a lecture that year described a striking fall in deaths on his wards. He later sprayed carbolic acid in the operating theatre, a method he eventually abandoned. Antisepsis met resistance, especially in Britain, but spread through Germany and elsewhere, and developed into modern aseptic surgery with sterilised instruments, gowns and gloves.
image_file: Lister, On the antiseptic principle...Lancet Wellcome L0000598.jpg
image_caption: Lister's article in The Lancet, 1867

title: Discovery of the tubercle bacillus
creator: koch
location: Imperial Health Office, Berlin; announced to the Berlin Physiological Society, 24 March 1882
note: Koch's identification of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis, then the leading cause of death in Europe.
description: Tuberculosis, also known as consumption, killed about one in seven people in nineteenth-century Europe, and many thought it hereditary. Koch developed a new staining method that made a tiny rod-shaped bacterium visible in tubercular tissue from humans and animals, grew it in pure culture on coagulated blood serum, which took weeks because it grows very slowly, and showed that injecting the culture into guinea pigs produced the disease. He announced the discovery at a meeting of the Berlin Physiological Society on 24 March 1882, a date now marked as World Tuberculosis Day, and published it as Die Ätiologie der Tuberculose. His systematic chain of proof became the model for linking a microbe to a disease, later formalised as Koch's postulates. His later claim that a substance from the bacilli, tuberculin, could cure the disease proved a costly failure, though it became a diagnostic test. Effective treatment came only with antibiotics after the Second World War.

title: On the Mode of Communication of Cholera and the Broad Street map
creator: john-snow
location: London: John Churchill
note: Snow's study showing that cholera spreads through contaminated water, with his map of deaths around the Broad Street pump.
description: Snow first set out his theory that cholera is spread by a poison or agent in contaminated water, not by bad air, in a pamphlet of 1849. When a violent outbreak killed over five hundred people in a few weeks in Soho in late August and September 1854, he investigated house by house and found that the deaths were concentrated around a public water pump in Broad Street, now Broadwick Street, while workers at a nearby brewery who drank beer and a workhouse with its own well were largely spared. He persuaded the local board to remove the pump's handle on 8 September, by which time the outbreak was already waning. In the second edition of his book in 1855 he published a map marking each death with a bar, which became a famous image, and the results of his 'grand experiment' comparing death rates among households supplied by two water companies, one drawing from sewage-polluted Thames water. The local curate Henry Whitehead, at first sceptical, traced the source to a baby's nappies washed into a leaking cesspool next to the well.
image_caption: Snow's map of cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump, 1854

title: Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East
creator: nightingale
location: London; published in Notes on Matters Affecting the Health, Efficiency and Hospital Administration of the British Army
note: Nightingale's polar-area 'rose' diagrams showing that preventable disease killed far more soldiers than wounds.
description: After the Crimean War, Nightingale worked with the statistician William Farr to analyse the deaths of British soldiers in the military hospitals at Scutari and in the Crimea. To make the findings unmistakable to officials and the public, she designed coloured diagrams, now usually called rose or coxcomb diagrams, in which each month is a wedge of a circle and the area of coloured sections shows the number of deaths from wounds, from other causes, and from 'zymotic', infectious, diseases such as cholera, typhus and dysentery. The large blue areas of preventable disease dwarfed the red of wounds, and the diagrams showed how deaths fell after a Sanitary Commission improved drains, ventilation and water in 1855. Polar-area charts had been used before, but her diagrams became the most famous early example of statistical graphics used for persuasion, and they helped bring about reforms in army health and the design of hospitals.
image_file: Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East. (IA dr diagram-of-the-causes-of-mortality-in-the-army-in-the-east-10563002).jpg
image_caption: Nightingale's rose diagram of causes of mortality, 1858

title: Drawings of neurons and the neuron doctrine
creator: cajal
location: Instituto Cajal, Madrid (Legado Cajal)
note: Cajal's detailed drawings of nerve cells, which showed that the nervous system is made of separate neurons.
description: In 1887 Cajal learned of the 'black reaction' discovered by Camillo Golgi, a silver stain that colours just a few nerve cells completely, revealing their branching shapes against a clear background. He improved it and applied it to the brains of young animals and birds, where cells were less tangled. In 1888 he published evidence, from the cerebellum, that the endings of nerve fibres touch other cells but do not fuse with them, so the nervous system is made of independent units, later called neurons, rather than a continuous net as Golgi and most others held. He proposed that nerve impulses travel in one direction, from the branching dendrites through the cell body to the axon. He set out his findings in his great Textura del sistema nervioso del hombre y de los vertebrados of 1899–1904, illustrated with thousands of drawings in ink and pencil, of the retina, cortex, spinal cord and other tissues, which combine scientific accuracy with remarkable beauty. The neuron doctrine was definitively confirmed by electron microscopy in the 1950s.
image_caption: Cajal's drawing of neurons in the cerebellum

title: History of penicillin: Fleming's discovery
creator: fleming
location: St Mary's Hospital, London; published in the British Journal of Experimental Pathology, 1929
note: Fleming noticed that a mould killed bacteria on a culture plate and named its active substance penicillin.
description: Returning from holiday in September 1928, Fleming examined culture plates of Staphylococcus bacteria that he had left on his bench at St Mary's Hospital and noticed that on one of them a contaminating mould was surrounded by a clear zone where the bacteria had been destroyed. He grew the mould, identified as Penicillium notatum, now Penicillium rubens, found that its broth killed many disease-causing bacteria but was harmless to white blood cells, and named the active substance penicillin. He published his findings in 1929 and used it as a laboratory tool for separating bacteria, but its instability and the difficulty of purifying it discouraged him from developing it as a drug. In 1939–41 Howard Florey, Ernst Chain, Norman Heatley and their colleagues in Oxford purified it, showed its spectacular effects in mice and then in patients, and with American industry developed mass production during the Second World War. His laboratory at St Mary's is now the Alexander Fleming Laboratory Museum.
image_file: Glass phial of British Standard penicillin, London, England, Wellcome L0059573.jpg
image_caption: Glass phial of British standard penicillin, Wellcome Collection

title: The Laws of Thought
creator: boole
location: London: Walton and Maberly; Cambridge: Macmillan
note: Boole's algebra of logic, in which reasoning is calculation with symbols taking the values 0 and 1.
description: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, on which are Founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probabilities developed ideas Boole had first published in 1847. He represented classes of things, or propositions, by letters such as x and y, the combination 'x and y' by multiplication and 'either x or y' by addition, with 1 standing for the universe of discourse and 0 for nothing. Because a class combined with itself is unchanged, x times x equals x, which holds only for the numbers 0 and 1, so logic becomes an algebra of those two values. With this system the syllogisms of traditional logic, and far more complex arguments, could be worked out by calculation. Boole also applied it to probability. His algebra was simplified by later logicians such as William Stanley Jevons and Charles Sanders Peirce, and in 1937 Claude Shannon showed that it describes electrical switching circuits, making it the foundation of digital computer design.

title: Difference Engine
creator: babbage
location: Science Museum, London; Computer History Museum, Mountain View (Difference Engine No. 2)
note: Babbage's design for a machine to calculate and print mathematical tables automatically, built only in modern times.
description: Mathematical tables of logarithms, astronomical positions and navigation were calculated by hand and full of errors. In 1822 Babbage proposed a machine that would compute tables by the method of finite differences, which needs only repeated addition, and print the results to avoid copying mistakes. With government money he employed the engineer Joseph Clement to build Difference Engine No. 1, but after disputes and costs of over £17,000 work stopped in 1833, leaving only a demonstration section of about 2,000 parts, which Babbage showed at his parties. Between 1847 and 1849 he designed a simpler and more elegant Difference Engine No. 2. Its plans lay unused until the Science Museum in London built it, completing the calculating section in 1991 for the bicentenary of Babbage's birth and the printer in 2002. It weighs about five tonnes, has some 8,000 parts and works exactly as he intended, proving that the design was sound. The Swedish engineers Georg and Edvard Scheutz built a working difference engine of their own in the 1850s.
image_caption: Babbage's Difference Engine

title: Analytical Engine
creator: babbage
type: Design for a mechanical general-purpose computer
location: Science Museum, London (trial model of the mill and printing mechanism)
note: Babbage's design for a programmable mechanical computer with a store, a mill and punched-card input.
description: From 1834 Babbage worked on a far more ambitious machine than the Difference Engine. The Analytical Engine was to have a 'store' holding a thousand numbers of fifty digits each, and a 'mill' that would perform arithmetic on numbers brought from the store, the equivalent of a modern computer's memory and central processor. It would be programmed by punched cards, borrowed from the Jacquard loom that wove patterns in silk, with separate cards for operations and for the addresses of variables, and it could make decisions by branching according to the results of calculations, and repeat sequences in loops. Output would be printed or punched. The engine was never built, partly for lack of funding; Babbage made thousands of pages of drawings and notes and built only small parts, and his son Henry assembled a piece of the mill after his death. It was a general-purpose computer in principle, a century before electronic computers, though there is little evidence that its designers in the 1940s were influenced by it.
image_caption: Trial model of part of the Analytical Engine, Science Museum, London

title: Notes on the Analytical Engine (Note G)
creator: lovelace
location: Scientific Memoirs, vol. 3, London: Richard and John E. Taylor
note: Lovelace's notes on Babbage's engine, with a program for Bernoulli numbers and a vision of computing beyond numbers.
description: In 1842 the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea published in French a description of the Analytical Engine based on lectures Babbage had given in Turin. Ada Lovelace translated it into English and, at Babbage's suggestion, added seven notes, labelled A to G, signed only with her initials A.A.L. In them she explained the difference between the Difference Engine and the Analytical Engine, how the engine could be instructed through cards, and the use of repeated sequences of operations. Note G gave a detailed table of the steps by which the engine could calculate Bernoulli numbers, often described as the first published computer program, though how much she and Babbage each contributed is debated. Most strikingly, she argued that the engine could act on any objects whose relations could be expressed by symbols, so that it might compose elaborate music, while adding that it could originate nothing and only do what it was ordered to perform, a remark that Alan Turing discussed as 'Lady Lovelace's objection'.
image_file: Diagram for the computation of Bernoulli numbers.jpg
image_caption: Lovelace's table for computing Bernoulli numbers, Note G, 1843

title: On the Hypotheses which Lie at the Foundations of Geometry
creator: riemann
location: University of Göttingen; published in the Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen
note: Riemann's lecture introducing curved spaces of any dimension, the geometry later used for general relativity.
description: For his habilitation, the qualification to teach in a German university, Riemann had to give a lecture on a topic chosen by the faculty from three he proposed, and Gauss, against custom, chose the third, on the foundations of geometry. Delivered on 10 June 1854 before an audience that mostly could not follow it, the lecture contained almost no formulas. Riemann described manifolds, spaces of any number of dimensions, and showed how their geometry could be determined by a rule for measuring distances between nearby points, so that curvature could vary from place to place. Euclidean geometry and the non-Euclidean geometries of Lobachevsky and Bolyai became special cases. He suggested that the geometry of physical space was a question for experience and might depend on the forces acting in it. The lecture was published only after his death, in 1868. The mathematics it opened, developed by Christoffel, Ricci and Levi-Civita, provided the language Einstein needed for general relativity.

title: On the Number of Primes Less Than a Given Magnitude
creator: riemann
location: Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, Berlin
note: Riemann's only paper on number theory, linking primes to the zeta function and stating the Riemann hypothesis.
description: Riemann wrote this eight-page paper on his election to the Berlin Academy. Taking the zeta function, which Euler had shown is related to the prime numbers, he extended it to complex numbers and showed how an exact formula for the number of primes up to any given size could be written in terms of the zeros of this function. He remarked, almost in passing, that it was very likely that all the non-trivial zeros lie on a single line in the complex plane, but that he had put aside the search for a proof. This statement, the Riemann hypothesis, would give the most precise possible information about how the primes are distributed. It was the eighth of Hilbert's problems in 1900 and is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems; billions of zeros have been checked by computer, but it remains unproved. The paper's methods were used in 1896 to prove the prime number theorem.

title: Cantor's diagonal argument and the theory of transfinite numbers
creator: cantor
location: Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik; Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung, 1891
note: Cantor's proofs that the real numbers are uncountable and that there is an endless hierarchy of infinite sizes.
description: In an 1874 paper with a deliberately modest title, Cantor proved that although the algebraic numbers can be listed one by one, like the whole numbers, the real numbers cannot: there are, in a precise sense, more points on a line than there are whole numbers. In 1891 he gave a simpler and more general proof, the diagonal argument: given any list of infinite sequences of digits, one can construct a new sequence that differs from the first in its first digit, from the second in its second, and so on, so it cannot be in the list. The same idea shows that the set of all subsets of any set is always larger than the set itself, so there is no largest infinity. In papers up to 1897 Cantor built an arithmetic of infinite cardinal and ordinal numbers. His work was attacked by some mathematicians as meaningless, and paradoxes found around 1900 led to the axiomatic set theory that now underlies most of mathematics. The diagonal method was later used by Gödel and Turing.
image_caption: Diagram of the diagonal argument

title: Hilbert's problems
creator: hilbert
location: International Congress of Mathematicians, Paris
note: Twenty-three unsolved problems presented by Hilbert in 1900, which shaped mathematical research in the twentieth century.
description: On 8 August 1900, at the second International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, Hilbert gave a lecture on the future of mathematics, arguing that every well-posed problem has a solution and that problems are the lifeblood of the subject. He presented ten problems in the lecture and published twenty-three in the printed version. They included Cantor's continuum hypothesis, the consistency of the axioms of arithmetic, the Riemann hypothesis, the axiomatisation of physics and the existence of an algorithm to decide whether a Diophantine equation has whole-number solutions. Over the following century work on them produced major advances: Gödel's and Paul Cohen's work showed that the continuum hypothesis cannot be decided from the usual axioms, Gödel's incompleteness theorems bore on the second problem, and Yuri Matiyasevich showed in 1970 that the tenth has no general solution. Some are solved, some were too vague to be settled, and some, including the Riemann hypothesis, remain open.

title: Discovery of X-rays (Hand mit Ringen)
creator: rontgen
location: University of Würzburg; published in the Sitzungsberichte der Physikalisch-Medizinischen Gesellschaft zu Würzburg
note: Röntgen's discovery of a penetrating radiation, announced with an X-ray image of his wife's hand.
description: On 8 November 1895, working alone in his laboratory at Würzburg with a cathode-ray tube covered in black cardboard, Röntgen noticed a faint glow on a screen coated with barium platinocyanide lying nearby. He spent seven weeks investigating the unknown rays, which he called X-rays, showing that they travel in straight lines, are not deflected by magnets, pass through paper, wood and flesh but are stopped by metals and bone, and darken photographic plates. On 22 December he made an image of the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, showing her bones and wedding ring; she is said to have exclaimed that she had seen her death. His paper On a New Kind of Rays, submitted on 28 December, and copies of the image sent to colleagues caused an international sensation. Within weeks X-rays were being used to locate bullets and set fractures. Their nature as short-wavelength electromagnetic radiation was shown by Max von Laue's diffraction experiments in 1912, which also founded X-ray crystallography. The dangers of overexposure were learned only slowly.
image_file: First medical X-ray by Wilhelm Röntgen of his wife Anna Bertha Ludwig's hand - 18951222.jpg
image_caption: Röntgen's X-ray image of his wife's hand, 22 December 1895

title: Discovery of polonium and radium
creator: marie-curie
location: École municipale de physique et chimie industrielles, Paris; announced in the Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences
note: Marie and Pierre Curie found two new radioactive elements in the uranium ore pitchblende.
description: For her doctoral research Marie Curie chose to study the rays from uranium discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896. Using an electrometer designed by Pierre Curie and his brother Jacques, she measured the faint electric currents the rays produced in air, and found that thorium also emits them and that the intensity depends only on the amount of the element, suggesting that it is a property of the atom; she called it radioactivity. Pitchblende, a uranium ore, was more active than its uranium content could explain, so she and Pierre, who abandoned his own research to join her, chemically separated it. In July 1898 they announced polonium, named after her occupied homeland, and in December, with Gustave Bémont, radium. Working in a leaky shed, Marie processed several tonnes of pitchblende residues to obtain a tenth of a gram of radium chloride in 1902 and determine its atomic weight. Radium became a sensation and was used in cancer treatment. Her notebooks are still so radioactive that they are kept in lead-lined boxes at the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
image_file: Pages from Marie Curie's notebook, Wellcome L0001764.jpg
image_caption: Pages from Marie Curie's laboratory notebook

title: Planck's radiation law and the quantum of action
creator: planck
location: Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft, Berlin; Annalen der Physik, 1901
note: Planck's formula for black-body radiation, which required energy to come in discrete packets: the birth of quantum theory.
description: A black body, an ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it, emits light with a spectrum that depends only on its temperature, and measurements at the Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt in Berlin in the 1890s gave precise data that no theory could fully explain. In October 1900 Planck found a formula that fitted the measurements perfectly at all wavelengths. To derive it, in a paper read to the German Physical Society on 14 December 1900, he had to assume that the oscillators emitting the radiation could only have energies in whole multiples of a small unit, proportional to frequency, with a constant of proportionality h, now called Planck's constant. Planck regarded this at first as a mathematical device and for years tried to reconcile it with classical physics. It was Einstein in 1905, treating light itself as made of quanta, and Bohr in 1913 who showed that quantisation was fundamental. Planck's constant is now one of the constants used to define the kilogram, since 2019.
image_caption: Black-body radiation curves at different temperatures

title: Rutherford model of the atom
creator: rutherford
location: University of Manchester; published in the Philosophical Magazine
note: Rutherford's interpretation of the gold-foil experiment: the atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus.
description: In 1909 at Manchester, Hans Geiger and the student Ernest Marsden, working under Rutherford, fired alpha particles from a radioactive source at a very thin gold foil and counted the flashes they made on a fluorescent screen. Most passed straight through, but about one in eight thousand bounced back at large angles. The prevailing 'plum pudding' model of J. J. Thomson, with electrons scattered through a diffuse sphere of positive charge, could not explain this; Rutherford later said it was as if a fifteen-inch shell had bounced back from tissue paper. In a paper of May 1911 he showed mathematically that the results fitted an atom with almost all its mass and positive charge concentrated in a minute central nucleus, with electrons at a great distance, so that the atom is mostly empty space. Geiger and Marsden confirmed his scattering formula in detail in 1913. The model was unstable according to classical physics, a problem that Bohr resolved with quantum theory, and it opened the way to nuclear physics.
image_caption: Diagram of the gold-foil experiment: expected and observed scattering

title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies (special relativity)
creator: einstein
location: Annalen der Physik, Leipzig
note: Einstein's paper on special relativity, showing that measurements of time and space depend on the observer's motion.
description: Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter Körper was received by the Annalen der Physik on 30 June 1905 and published in September, one of four papers that made 1905 Einstein's 'miracle year'. Starting from two postulates, that the laws of physics are the same for all observers moving uniformly, and that light always travels at the same speed in empty space regardless of the motion of its source, Einstein showed that the ideas of absolute time and simultaneity must be abandoned. Moving clocks run slow and moving rods are shortened in their direction of motion, as seen by a stationary observer, and the transformations between observers' measurements, found earlier by Lorentz in a different interpretation, follow simply. The ether, the supposed medium of light, becomes superfluous. In a short follow-up paper later that year Einstein showed that a body's mass is a measure of its energy content, the relation usually written E = mc². In 1908 Hermann Minkowski reformulated the theory as a geometry of four-dimensional spacetime.

title: On a Heuristic Point of View Concerning the Production and Transformation of Light
creator: einstein
location: Annalen der Physik, Leipzig
note: Einstein's proposal that light consists of quanta of energy, explaining the photoelectric effect.
description: In this paper, received in March 1905, Einstein proposed that light, despite all the evidence that it is a wave, behaves in some situations as if it consists of independent packets, or quanta, of energy proportional to its frequency, extending Planck's quantum hypothesis from matter to radiation itself. He applied the idea to the photoelectric effect, in which light falling on a metal surface ejects electrons: experiments by Philipp Lenard had shown that the electrons' energy depends on the light's colour, not its brightness, which wave theory could not explain. Einstein predicted a simple linear relation between frequency and electron energy. The idea was received with great scepticism, even by Planck, and Robert Millikan set out to disprove the relation, but confirmed it precisely in 1914–16. It was for this work, rather than relativity, that Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. The light quanta, later called photons, were central to quantum mechanics and the idea of wave-particle duality.

title: General theory of relativity
creator: einstein
location: Prussian Academy of Sciences, Berlin; Annalen der Physik, 1916
note: Einstein's theory of gravity as the curvature of spacetime, confirmed by the bending of starlight in 1919.
description: From 1907, when he realised that a person falling freely would not feel their own weight, Einstein worked to extend relativity to accelerated motion and gravity. With the help of his friend the mathematician Marcel Grossmann he learned Riemann's geometry and the tensor calculus, and after years of false starts presented the final field equations to the Prussian Academy in Berlin in November 1915, publishing a full account in the Annalen der Physik in 1916. In general relativity, matter and energy curve spacetime, and bodies move along the straightest possible paths in the curved geometry, which appears to us as gravitational attraction. The theory explained the long-standing anomaly in the orbit of Mercury and predicted that light passing the Sun would be deflected by twice the Newtonian amount; the British eclipse expeditions led by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson in 1919 reported confirmation, making Einstein world-famous. Its later predictions, the expansion of the universe, black holes, gravitational lensing and gravitational waves, first detected directly in 2015, have all been confirmed.

title: On the Constitution of Atoms and Molecules (Bohr model)
creator: bohr
location: Philosophical Magazine, London
note: Bohr's quantum model of the atom, in which electrons occupy fixed orbits and emit light when they jump between them.
description: In a trilogy of papers published in 1913, Bohr combined Rutherford's nuclear atom with Planck's quantum. He postulated that the electron in a hydrogen atom can circle the nucleus only in certain stationary orbits, in which it does not radiate as classical physics would require, and that it emits or absorbs light of a single frequency when it jumps from one orbit to another, the energy of the light being the difference between the energies of the orbits. From these assumptions he derived the Balmer formula for the lines in the hydrogen spectrum, known empirically since 1885, and calculated the Rydberg constant from fundamental constants, a striking success. The model also explained spectra of ionised helium and the general structure of the periodic table. It could not explain atoms with more than one electron or the intensities of spectral lines, and was replaced by quantum mechanics in the 1920s, but its picture of an atom with electrons in shells remains a common teaching image.
image_caption: Diagram of the Bohr model of the atom

title: Invariante Variationsprobleme (Noether's theorem)
creator: noether
location: Nachrichten von der Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen
note: Noether's proof that every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conservation law.
description: Hilbert and Klein had asked Noether to help them understand a puzzle in general relativity: energy did not seem to be conserved in the usual way. In this paper, presented to the Göttingen society by Klein in July 1918 because she was not a member, Noether proved two general theorems about systems described by a principle of least action. The first shows that every continuous symmetry of such a system corresponds to a conserved quantity: if the laws are unchanged by shifts in time, energy is conserved; by shifts in space, momentum; by rotations, angular momentum. The second explains why in theories like general relativity, whose symmetries depend on arbitrary functions, conservation laws take a different form. The first theorem became one of the most important tools of twentieth-century physics, used throughout quantum field theory and the Standard Model of particle physics, where conserved quantities such as electric charge are traced to symmetries. Einstein praised her penetrating mathematical thinking.
image_caption: First page of Noether's paper, 1918

title: Matrix mechanics and the uncertainty principle
creator: heisenberg
location: Zeitschrift für Physik, Berlin
note: Heisenberg's first formulation of quantum mechanics, and his principle that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
description: Suffering from hay fever, Heisenberg went to the treeless North Sea island of Heligoland in June 1925 and there worked out a new mechanics for atoms that used only observable quantities, such as the frequencies and intensities of spectral lines, rather than unobservable electron orbits. His paper, published in July 1925, contained a strange rule of multiplication in which the order of factors mattered; Max Born recognised it as matrix algebra, and Born, Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan developed matrix mechanics into a complete theory by the end of the year. In 1927, working in Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, Heisenberg showed that the theory implies that the more precisely the position of a particle is determined, the less precisely its momentum can be known, and vice versa, with the product of the uncertainties never smaller than a quantity set by Planck's constant. The uncertainty principle became a cornerstone of the Copenhagen interpretation, and Heisenberg received the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1932.

title: Quantisation as an Eigenvalue Problem (Schrödinger equation)
creator: schrodinger
location: Annalen der Physik, Leipzig
note: Schrödinger's wave equation, which describes how the quantum state of a system evolves and gives atomic energy levels.
description: Inspired by Louis de Broglie's suggestion that electrons have wave properties, Schrödinger sought an equation for these matter waves, and over the Christmas holiday of 1925, in a villa in Arosa in the Swiss Alps, found it. In four papers published in the first half of 1926 he showed that the allowed energy levels of the hydrogen atom follow naturally as the frequencies at which the electron wave can vibrate in a stable pattern, much as a guitar string can vibrate only at certain notes. Unlike Heisenberg's matrices, his wave mechanics used familiar mathematics of differential equations and was quickly adopted. He also showed that the two theories were mathematically equivalent. Schrödinger hoped that the wave represented a real smeared-out electron, but Max Born proposed in 1926 that the square of its size gives the probability of finding the particle at a place, the interpretation that prevailed. The Schrödinger equation is the basic equation of quantum chemistry, materials science and much of modern physics.

title: What Is Life?
creator: schrodinger
location: Trinity College, Dublin (lectures, 1943); Cambridge University Press
note: Schrödinger's lectures asking how physics and chemistry can explain life, which inspired the founders of molecular biology.
description: In February 1943 Schrödinger gave three public lectures at Trinity College, Dublin, published the following year as What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell. Drawing on the work of the geneticist Max Delbrück and his colleagues on mutations caused by X-rays, he argued that the hereditary material must be a very small but extremely stable molecular structure, an 'aperiodic crystal' whose arrangement of atoms forms a 'code-script' determining the development of the organism. He also discussed how living things maintain their order against the tendency to disorder by drawing 'negative entropy' from their surroundings. Many of the ideas were not new, and biologists have criticised some of them, but the short book, written for a general audience, made the physical problem of heredity exciting to physicists. James Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins all said it influenced their decision to work on genes.

title: Hubble's law of galaxy recession
creator: hubble
location: Mount Wilson Observatory; published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
note: Hubble's evidence that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to their distance, the basis of the expanding universe.
description: In 1924–25 Hubble had shown that the spiral nebulae are distant galaxies by finding Cepheid variable stars in them, whose regular pulsations reveal their true brightness and hence their distance. In a short paper of 1929, A Relation between Distance and Radial Velocity among Extra-Galactic Nebulae, he plotted the distances of 24 galaxies against their velocities, most of them measured from redshifts in their spectra by Vesto Slipher at Lowell Observatory, and found a roughly linear relation: the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is receding. With Milton Humason he extended the relation to much greater distances in 1931. Hubble was cautious about the interpretation, but the relation was soon understood as evidence that the universe is expanding, as Georges Lemaître had predicted from general relativity in 1927. Hubble's distances were too small by a large factor, giving too young an age for the universe, a problem corrected in the 1950s. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended calling it the Hubble–Lemaître law.
image_file: Snapshots of the star that changed the Universe (opo1115d).jpg
image_caption: Hubble Space Telescope images of V1, the Cepheid in Andromeda that Hubble identified in 1923

title: The primeval atom and the expanding universe
creator: lemaitre
location: Annales de la Société Scientifique de Bruxelles, 1927; Nature, 1931
note: Lemaître's proposals that the universe is expanding and that it began from a single 'primeval atom', the origin of the Big Bang theory.
description: In 1927 Lemaître published in a Belgian journal a paper showing that Einstein's equations of general relativity allow a universe of constant mass with a growing radius, and that this would account for the recession of the galaxies; using published distances and velocities, he derived an expansion rate close to the one Hubble found two years later. Einstein reportedly told him that his calculations were correct but his physics abominable. The paper was little noticed until Eddington arranged for an English translation in 1931, in which the passage estimating the expansion rate was omitted, a fact that later prompted speculation but was shown in 2011 to be Lemaître's own decision. In a letter to Nature in 1931, Lemaître went further and suggested that the universe began as a single quantum, a 'primeval atom', which split into the matter of the cosmos. The idea, mocked as the 'Big Bang' by Fred Hoyle in 1949, was developed by George Gamow and colleagues and confirmed by the discovery of the cosmic microwave background in 1965.
image_caption: Diagram of the history of the expanding universe (NASA)

title: On a Remarkable Bacteriolytic Element Found in Tissues and Secretions (lysozyme)
creator: fleming
location: Proceedings of the Royal Society B, London
note: Fleming's discovery of lysozyme, a natural antibacterial enzyme in tears, saliva and mucus.
description: In 1921, while suffering from a cold, Fleming added a drop of his own nasal mucus to a culture plate of bacteria and later noticed that the bacteria around it had dissolved. He went on to show that a similar substance was present in tears, saliva, egg white, blood and many tissues, and named it lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria. He published the discovery in 1922. Lysozyme mostly attacks harmless bacteria and was of little use as a drug, but the experience of looking for natural substances that kill bacteria prepared Fleming to recognise the significance of the contaminating mould he found in 1928. Lysozyme later became important in research: it was the first enzyme whose three-dimensional structure was determined, by David Phillips's group in 1965, and it is part of the body's innate defence against infection.

title: On Formally Undecidable Propositions (incompleteness theorems)
creator: godel
location: Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik, Vienna
note: Gödel's proof that any consistent formal system that includes arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
description: Gödel's paper Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme, received in November 1930 and published in 1931, answered a central question of Hilbert's programme. Gödel showed how statements about a formal system, such as 'this formula is provable', can be encoded as statements about numbers within the system itself, by assigning a number to every symbol, formula and proof. He then constructed a statement that in effect says of itself that it is not provable. If the system is consistent, this statement can be neither proved nor disproved within it, and so is true but unprovable. This is the first incompleteness theorem. The second shows that such a system cannot prove its own consistency. The results apply to any system strong enough to express basic arithmetic, including the Principia Mathematica of Whitehead and Russell. They ended the hope of a complete and self-certifying foundation for mathematics, influenced Turing's work on computability and remain among the most discussed results in logic and philosophy.

title: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
creator: turing
location: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society
note: Turing's paper defining the Turing machine and the universal machine, and showing that some problems cannot be solved by computation.
description: Hilbert had asked whether there is a definite mechanical procedure that can decide, for any statement of mathematical logic, whether it is provable, the Entscheidungsproblem or decision problem. To answer, Turing, aged twenty-three, analysed what a human computer does when calculating with pencil and paper, and reduced it to a simple abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape, one square at a time, following a finite table of rules. He showed that there is a universal machine that, given the description of any other machine on its tape, can imitate it, the essential idea of the stored-program computer. He then proved that no machine can decide, for every machine, whether it will ever print a certain symbol, a result related to what is now called the halting problem, and concluded that the decision problem has no solution. Alonzo Church had reached the same conclusion by a different method shortly before. The Turing machine became the standard definition of computation and the foundation of computer science.

title: The Bombe
creator: turing
location: Bletchley Park, Buckinghamshire (working reconstruction at The National Museum of Computing)
note: The machine designed by Turing, improved by Gordon Welchman, that found the daily settings of the German Enigma cipher.
description: The German armed forces enciphered their messages with Enigma machines whose rotors and plugboard settings were changed daily, giving an astronomical number of possibilities. Polish mathematicians led by Marian Rejewski had broken early Enigma traffic and built a machine called the bomba, and shared their methods with Britain and France in July 1939. At Bletchley Park, Turing designed a much more powerful and general machine that tested possible rotor settings against a 'crib', a guessed fragment of plain text, using chains of logical deductions to eliminate impossible settings quickly. Gordon Welchman added the 'diagonal board', which greatly increased its power. The first Bombe, named Victory, began work in March 1940, built by the British Tabulating Machine Company, and over two hundred were in use by the end of the war, operated mostly by members of the Women's Royal Naval Service. The intelligence obtained, code-named Ultra, was vital in the Battle of the Atlantic. All the Bombes were dismantled after the war; a working reconstruction was completed in 2006.

title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
creator: turing
location: Mind, Oxford
note: Turing's paper proposing the imitation game, now known as the Turing test, as a way of asking whether machines can think.
description: Turing opens this paper by proposing to replace the question 'Can machines think?', which he regarded as too vague to discuss, with a game: an interrogator communicates by typed messages with a human and a machine and tries to tell which is which. If the machine can play the imitation game as well as a human, he suggests, there is no good reason to deny that it thinks. He then explains what digital computers are and why one could in principle imitate any discrete machine, and answers nine objections, including theological ones, the argument from consciousness, the mathematical objection from Gödel's theorem and Lady Lovelace's objection that a machine can only do what it is told. He predicts that by about the end of the century machines would play the game well enough that general opinion would accept talk of machines thinking. He ends by proposing that, rather than programming an adult mind, it would be better to build a 'child machine' and educate it, an early statement of the idea of machine learning. The paper is a founding text of artificial intelligence.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
creator: shannon
location: Bell System Technical Journal, New York
note: Shannon's paper founding information theory, defining the bit and the capacity of a communication channel.
description: Published in two parts in the Bell System Technical Journal in July and October 1948, Shannon's paper set out a general mathematical model of communication: a source produces a message, a transmitter encodes it into a signal, the signal passes through a channel where noise may corrupt it, and a receiver decodes it for its destination. He defined the information produced by a source as a measure of its uncertainty, which he called entropy by analogy with physics, and measured it in binary digits, or bits, a term he credited to John Tukey. He proved that messages can be compressed down to their entropy and no further, and that every noisy channel has a capacity: below that rate, information can be transmitted with an arbitrarily small rate of error by suitable coding, while above it reliable communication is impossible. These results gave engineers the limits within which they worked and the goals to aim for, and they underlie data compression, error-correcting codes, mobile telephones, the internet and space communication. The paper was republished as a book with Warren Weaver in 1949.

title: Photo 51
creator: rosalind-franklin
location: King's College London; published in Nature, 25 April 1953
note: The X-ray diffraction image of B-form DNA, made in Franklin's laboratory, whose cross pattern showed a helix.
description: At King's College London, Franklin and her doctoral student Raymond Gosling found that DNA fibres take two forms depending on humidity, a dry crystalline A form and a wet B form, and they made very fine X-ray diffraction photographs of each. Photograph number 51, of the B form, was taken in May 1952 after an exposure of many hours. Its striking X-shaped pattern of spots indicated a helical structure, and the spacing of the layers gave its dimensions. In January 1953, after Franklin had decided to leave King's, Gosling passed the photograph to Maurice Wilkins, who showed it to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge. Watson later wrote that his mouth fell open and his pulse began to race. With Franklin's measurements, which reached Crick through a Medical Research Council report, it helped Watson and Crick build their model. The photograph was published with an article by Franklin and Gosling in the same issue of Nature as the Watson and Crick paper, and has become a symbol both of the discovery and of the debate about credit for it.

title: Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid
creator: watson
location: Nature, London, 25 April 1953
note: The one-page paper by Watson and Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA.
description: Working at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, Watson and Crick built physical models from wire and metal plates to find a structure that fitted the chemical facts about DNA and the X-ray evidence. After a failed triple-helix model in 1951, and with the help of Franklin's Photo 51 and measurements and Erwin Chargaff's finding that DNA contains equal amounts of adenine and thymine and of guanine and cytosine, they arrived at the final model in early March 1953. In it two chains of sugars and phosphates wind around each other in opposite directions, with the bases on the inside joined in pairs, adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine, by hydrogen bonds. The paper, little more than a page with a single diagram drawn by Crick's wife Odile, ends with a famously understated sentence noting that the specific pairing immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material. It appeared with supporting papers from Wilkins's and Franklin's groups. The structure explained how genes can be copied and how they can carry information, and it launched molecular biology. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in 1962.

title: On Protein Synthesis (the central dogma)
creator: crick
location: Symposia of the Society for Experimental Biology, Cambridge
note: Crick's statement of the sequence hypothesis and the central dogma: genetic information flows from nucleic acid to protein.
description: In a lecture given at University College London in September 1957 and published in 1958, Crick set out a framework for how the information stored in DNA is used to make proteins, at a time when the details were almost entirely unknown. The sequence hypothesis proposed that the order of bases in a stretch of nucleic acid specifies the order of amino acids in a protein, and that this sequence alone determines how the protein folds. The central dogma, as he called it, stated that once information has passed into protein it cannot get out again: information may flow from nucleic acid to nucleic acid or from nucleic acid to protein, but not from protein to protein or from protein back to nucleic acid. He also proposed that small 'adaptor' molecules carry amino acids to the template, a prediction soon fulfilled by the discovery of transfer RNA. The framework guided the research of the following decade, in which the genetic code was deciphered. The discovery of reverse transcription in 1970 added a flow from RNA to DNA that Crick had allowed for.
